blocks.meier-para-1: The doctrine of reason or the art of reason (logica, philosophia instrumentalis, philosophia rationalis) is a science that treats of the rules of learned cognition and of learned presentation.
blocks.meier-para-2: So that the doctrine of reason may contain no wholly arbitrary, contrived and unnatural laws, its rules must be derived 1) from the experiences of the effects of human reason, 2) from the nature of human reason, 3) from the general fundamental truths on which all human cognition rests.
blocks.meier-para-3: The aim of the doctrine of reason is either the perfection of a learned cognition and of a learned presentation, which suit only professional scholars, or which are also fitting and useful for other learned persons.
blocks.meier-para-4: The doctrine of reason is a means without which no learned cognition and science can be attained, and through whose proper use a learned cognition and science is attained §.1.
blocks.meier-para-5: Philosophy (philosophia) is a science of the more general properties of things, insofar as they are cognized without faith. Since learned cognition and learned presentation now comprise many kinds under themselves, their perfections and imperfections are more general properties of things, which are fully proved in the doctrine of reason without deriving their truth from testimony. The doctrine of reason is accordingly a part of philosophy.
blocks.meier-para-6: The doctrine of reason treats either of a wholly certain learned cognition and the presentation of it, or of probable learned cognition and the presentation of it §.1. The former is the doctrine of reason of wholly certain learned cognition (analytica), and the latter the doctrine of reason of probable learned cognition (dialectica, logica probabilium). We treat of the first doctrine of reason.
blocks.meier-para-7: In the doctrine of reason, the rules of learned cognition and of learned presentation are either applied to their particular kinds or not. The former is the practicing doctrine of reason (logica practica, utens) and the latter the teaching doctrine of reason (logica theoretica, docens).
blocks.meier-para-8: When the doctrine of reason is constituted as it can and must be by virtue of its nature, it has, among others, a threefold utility. 1) It promotes the learning and dissemination of all sciences, and of learnedness as a whole. Every student should therefore properly begin with the learning of the doctrine of reason. 2) It improves the understanding and reason, and shows how these powers of cognition must be used in order to cognize the truth in a proper manner. 3) It promotes virtue as a whole, in that it improves the free will; provides that cognition on which virtue rests; and has an indispensable influence on the improvement of conscience.
blocks.meier-para-9: The doctrine of reason treats I. Of learned cognition. 1. Of learned cognition in general. 2. Of the extensiveness of learned cognition. 3. Of the magnitude of learned cognition. 4. Of the truth of learned cognition. 5. Of the clarity of learned cognition. 6. Of the certainty of learned cognition. 7. Of practical learned cognition. 8. Of learned concepts. 9. Of learned judgments. 10. Of learned inferences of reason. II. Of the method of learned cognition. III. Of learned presentation. 1. Of the use of words. 2. Of the learned style of writing. 3. Of a learned speech. 4. Of learned writings. IV. Of the character of a scholar. The doctrine of reason. Of learned cognition. Of learned cognition in general.
blocks.meier-para-10: Experience teaches that we represent to ourselves infinitely many things. A representation (repraesentatio perceptio) behaves as a picture, which the painterly skill of the soul draws in its interior.
blocks.meier-para-11: Cognition (cognitio) is either a sum total of many representations, or that action through which a representation of a thing is effected. One may also, without fearing a noticeable error, hold representations and cognition to be one and the same.
blocks.meier-para-12: Distinct from representation and cognition is that which we represent to ourselves and which we cognize. The latter is called the object of cognition and of representation (obiectum cognitionis et repraesentationis).
blocks.meier-para-13: We are conscious of our representations and of our cognition (conscium esse, adpercipere) insofar as we distinguish them and their object from other representations and things. Consciousness is a double representation: a representation of the object, and a representation of its difference from others. Consciousness behaves like light in the corporeal world, which discloses to us the difference of bodies.
blocks.meier-para-14: When we are conscious of a representation, we are conscious of it either merely as considered as a whole, so that we distinguish nothing from one another in it itself; or we are also conscious of the manifold in it. In the first case we have an indistinct or a confused cognition (cognitio indistincta et confusa), in the other, however, a distinct one (cognitio distincta); for example, when we see a human being from afar, we have an indistinct cognition of his face for as long as we do not catch sight of the parts and features of the face. But if he comes nearer to us, and we begin to become aware of his eyes, his nose and the features of his face, we attain a distinct cognition of his face.
blocks.meier-para-15: That from which a thing, be it either a cognition or the object of one, can be cognized, is its ground (ratio), and what can be cognized from the ground is its consequence (rationatum). Light is the ground of the visibility of bodies, and this visibility is a consequence of light. The connection of things (nexus, consequentia) consists in this, when the one is the ground of the other, or contains it in itself. The ground of a thing is either so constituted that we can derive our whole cognition of it from it, such that nothing further besides it is required in order to cognize everything found in the thing; or it is not so constituted. The former is the sufficient ground (ratio sufficiens), and the latter the insufficient ground (ratio insufficiens).
blocks.meier-para-16: Everything that is possible and actual has a ground, and everything also has a sufficient ground.
blocks.meier-para-17: When we cognize something, we cognize it either in a distinct manner from grounds, or not. If the first is the case, we have a rational cognition (cognitio rationalis). Three things are required for such a cognition: 1) a cognition of a thing, 2) a cognition of its ground, and 3) a distinct cognition of the connection of the thing with its ground. For example: when I cognize that all human beings can err because they have a limited understanding, and I think: whoever has a limited understanding can err; now all human beings have a limited understanding, therefore they can all err: then I have a rational cognition of the truth that all human beings can err.
blocks.meier-para-18: Every cognition, insofar as it is not rational, is called a common or a historical cognition (cognitio vulgaris, historica). All things can be cognized historically, and one may even cognize their grounds; so long as one does not distinctly see the connection of the consequences with their grounds, one has only a merely historical cognition.
blocks.meier-para-19: A more perfect historical cognition is a beautiful cognition (cognitio pulcra, aesthetica), and the beautiful sciences occupy themselves with the rules through whose observance historical cognition is beautified.
blocks.meier-para-20: Although historical cognition is very different from rational cognition §.17. 18, such that the most beautiful historical cognition does not even deserve to be called a rational cognition §.19; yet the former is indispensable to the latter, in that a human being cannot attain a rational cognition of a thing unless he previously possesses a historical cognition of it.
blocks.meier-para-21: Learned and philosophical cognition (cognitio erudita et philosophica) is a rational cognition that is perfect in a higher or more noticeable degree.
blocks.meier-para-22: When the manifold in a cognition agrees toward an aim, or contains the sufficient ground of it: the perfection of cognition (perfectio cognitionis) consists in this. The perfections of cognition occur either in it insofar as it is distinct or insofar as it is indistinct §.14. The former are called the logical perfections of cognition (perfectio cognitionis logica), and the latter the beauties of it (pulcritudo et perfectio aesthetica cognitionis). E.g. mathematical certainty is a logical perfection, and painterly liveliness a beauty of cognition.
blocks.meier-para-23: Insofar as a cognition is not perfect, insofar it is an imperfect cognition (imperfectio cognitionis). The imperfections of cognition occur either in it insofar as it is distinct, or insofar as it is indistinct §.14. The former are called the logical imperfections of cognition (imperfectio cognitionis logica), and the latter the uglinesses of it (deformitas, imperfectio cognitionis aesthetica). E.g. the swinish and bawdy in everyday jests is an ugliness of cognition; a false inference of reason, however, is a logical imperfection of it.
blocks.meier-para-24: Learned cognition must be adorned with the perfections of cognition §.21. 22. Consequently it possesses either merely the logical perfections of cognition, in that it is either not beautiful at all or is at the same time even ugly; or it possesses, besides the logical perfections, the beauties of cognition §.22. 23. The former is a merely learned cognition (cognitio mere erudita), and the latter a cognition that is beautiful and learned at the same time (cognitio aesthetico-logica). The latter is more perfect than the former, and the former must not be sought alone.
blocks.meier-para-25: The more we cognize, the more perfect is our cognition §.22. The first perfection of learned cognition therefore consists in its extensiveness (vastitas, ubertas cognitionis eruditae), which is ascribed to a cognition insofar as it represents many objects to us.
blocks.meier-para-26: The greater and more important our cognition is, the more perfect it is, because a great thing comprehends much in itself §.22. The second perfection of learned cognition accordingly consists in its magnitude and importance (dignitas, magnitudo et maiestas cognitionis eruditae), which belongs to a cognition insofar as it is great and important. E.g. the cognition of God is more important than the cognition of the clothes of the Romans.
blocks.meier-para-27: Because a false cognition is no cognition at all, the truth of cognition (veritas cognitionis eruditae) is the third perfection of it. It can be called the fundamental perfection of cognition, because without it the cognition is no cognition at all, and hence also not capable of any perfection.
blocks.meier-para-28: Since in a distinct representation we represent to ourselves more than in an indistinct one §.14, the distinctness of learned cognition is the fourth perfection of it §.25.
blocks.meier-para-29: The consciousness of the truth of a cognition is its certainty (certitudo subiective spectata). Since now both the truth of cognition and the consciousness of it are a perfection §.13. 17, the certainty of learned cognition is the fifth perfection of it.
blocks.meier-para-30: A learned cognition is practical insofar as it contributes its share to the arrangement of our free actions (cognitio erudita practica), and in this consists the sixth perfection of it §.22.
blocks.meier-para-31: The more extensive, important, correct, distinct, certain and practical a learned cognition is, the more perfect it is §.25-30. Since now every rational human being must at all times strive toward the greatest perfection that is possible for him; so, if he strives to attain a learned cognition, he must 1) seek to reach all logical perfections of it, 2) each of them in the highest possible degree, and besides this 3) the beauties of cognition §.22.
blocks.meier-para-32: Whoever accordingly wants to attain the most perfect learned cognition must not be content with a merely learned cognition §.24. 31. Rather, although not all his learned representations can be beautiful at the same time, his learned cognition, considered as a whole, must nevertheless at the same time be a beautiful cognition, if it is to be improved to as high a degree as is possible.
blocks.meier-para-33: A learned cognition can 1) be logically perfect and imperfect at the same time. E.g. a correct, distinct and certain cognition can have the fault that it is not practical; 2) be logically perfect in a higher degree than imperfect, or more imperfect than perfect; 3) be logically perfect and beautiful or ugly at the same time; 4) be logically perfect and neither beautiful nor ugly; 5) be logically imperfect and at the same time beautiful or ugly §.22. 23.
blocks.meier-para-34: Whoever wants to attain a learned cognition that is at the same time beautiful §.32 must 1) not make it logically perfect in such a manner and to such a degree that all beauty of it is thereby prevented; 2) he must not beautify it in such a manner and to such a degree that the required logical perfection of it is thereby made impossible; 3) he must seek chiefly to preserve the logical perfections, and he must introduce the beauties only more sparingly, as an ornament.
blocks.meier-para-35: If some perfections in learned cognition cannot be attained at the same time, one must let go the smaller and less necessary perfections in order to retain the greater and more necessary ones. Accordingly, in a learned cognition that is not to be merely learned, one must often relax logical strictness in trifles in order to attain the greater beauty of cognition.
blocks.meier-para-36: The imperfections of learned cognition are either deficiencies or faults. A deficiency of learned cognition (defectus cognitionis eruditae) arises when certain rules of its perfection are neither observed nor transgressed. E.g. when a principal concept is not explained at all, the rules of explanations are neither observed nor transgressed. A fault of learned cognition (vitium cognitionis eruditae) arises when the rules of its perfection are transgressed. E.g. when one explains a concept falsely. Although one must avoid all deficiencies and faults, one must nevertheless guard more against the latter, because one can say that every fault is bound up with a deficiency, and a fault is accordingly a greater imperfection than a mere deficiency.
blocks.meier-para-37: Common and historical cognition can be much more perfect than the merely learned, namely when it is very beautiful §.22.23. E.g. an unlearned general and minister can possess a much more perfect cognition than a learned and pedantic bookworm. This advantage belongs to common cognition only accidentally, when the learned cognition is not as perfect as it could and should be.
blocks.meier-para-38: Learned cognition is always necessarily more perfect than common cognition, when they are equal to each other in the remaining respects §.18. 21.
blocks.meier-para-39: Although common cognition is very useful, and in infinitely many cases sufficient to promote our welfare, indeed although some common cognition can accidentally be more useful than some learned cognition: yet learned cognition is necessarily more useful than common, when they are equal to each other in the remaining respects. For 1) since it is more perfect §.38, it also improves the power of cognition in a higher degree than the common; 2) for the very same reason it affords a greater pleasure than the common; 3) it is more fitting and more becoming to the character of humanity than the common; 4) it promotes the discovery of new truths more than the common; and 5) it can be applied and practiced much more skillfully and better than common cognition.
blocks.meier-para-40: A learned cognition that is at the same time beautiful affords all the utilities of the learned §.39, and all the utilities of beautiful cognition. And since it at the same time prevents all the harm of the merely learned and of the merely beautiful cognition: it is among all kinds of human cognition the most useful and serviceable cognition. Of the extensiveness of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-41: The imperfection of learned cognition that is opposed to its extensiveness §.25 is the paltriness of learned cognition (angustia eruditae cognitionis), and it always arises from ignorance (ignorantia) or from the total lack of cognition of things and of their grounds. To the degree that the extensiveness of a human being's learned cognition increases, his ignorance decreases, and the greater a human being's ignorance is, the more paltry is his learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-42: A twofold ignorance is opposed to the extensiveness of learned cognition: 1) a total ignorance (ignorantia totalis), when we do not even have a historical cognition of a thing; and 2) an ignorance of the grounds of things (ignorantia rationum), in which an excellent historical cognition of them can still take place.
blocks.meier-para-43: A human being's ignorance is 1) an absolutely necessary and unavoidable ignorance (ignorantia absolute necessaria et invincibilis), which he cannot avoid on account of the limits of his power of cognition; and 2) a voluntary one (ignorantia arbitraria et vincibilis), the opposite cognition of which he could attain if he wished.
blocks.meier-para-44: The sum total of all those things which a human being can cognize in a learned manner without detriment to the rest of his entire perfection is the horizon, or the field of vision, of his learned cognition (horizon seu sphaera cognitionis eruditae). All things are therefore excluded from it with respect to which a human being must remain ignorant, whether of necessity or voluntarily §.43.
blocks.meier-para-45: A thing is elevated above the horizon of human learned cognition (res supra horizontem eruditae cognitionis humanae posita) when ignorance of it in a human being is absolutely necessary, although it is not unworthy of a learned cognition. The human understanding is too weak to be in a position to cognize these important things in a learned manner. Although now one must not despise such things as go beyond our horizon, and although one must not without sufficient ground pass off as a thing something that is elevated above the horizon of our cognition; yet one must seek as far as possible to avoid the vain and harmful striving after a learned cognition of such things as go beyond our horizon.
blocks.meier-para-46: A thing is lowered beneath the horizon of human learned cognition (res infra horizontem eruditae cognitionis humanae posita) which indeed could be cognized by a human being in a learned manner, but which is not great enough to be worth such a cognition. Just as one must not without sufficient ground pass off a thing as something that is lowered beneath the horizon of human learned cognition, so one must also not trouble oneself to cognize in a learned manner such things as are actually lowered beneath the horizon of human learned cognition. Otherwise one makes oneself ridiculous and contemptible, and neglects thereby the learned cognition of more important and more necessary things.
blocks.meier-para-47: A thing is outside the horizon of learned human cognition (res extra horizontem cognitionis humanae eruditae posita) which indeed could be cognized by a human being in a learned manner, which is also not unworthy of a human learned cognition, but whose learned cognition would hinder a human being in his remaining occupations. No one must without sufficient ground pass off a thing as something that is found outside the horizon of his learned cognition; but also no one must strive after a learned cognition of such things as are located outside the horizon of his learned cognition, because otherwise he would meddle in foreign affairs, and neglect his own work thereby.
blocks.meier-para-48: All those things which are neither elevated above the horizon of human learned cognition, nor lowered beneath it, nor found outside it, are located within the compass of the horizon of human learned cognition (res intra horizontem cognitionis humanae eruditae posita), and they constitute the learned horizon §.44.
blocks.meier-para-49: The most extensive learned cognition of a human being consists in the learned cognition of all things that are located within the compass of his horizon §.48. 25. Since now every scholar must attain the most extensive learned cognition that is possible for him; he must seek to measure out the limits and compass of his horizon as exactly as the weakness of human beings permits §.44.
blocks.meier-para-50: And even if a human being should have attained the most extensive learned cognition, much necessary ignorance still remains, which redounds to him neither to honor nor to disgrace §.43. But as for voluntary ignorance, it is either praiseworthy or blameworthy. Praiseworthy ignorance (ignorantia laudabilis) is the ignorance of such things as are found beneath and outside the horizon of learned cognition §.46.47.
blocks.meier-para-51: Blameworthy ignorance (ignorantia illaudabilis) is the ignorance of such things as are found within the horizon of learned cognition §.48. Whoever therefore wants to attain the most extensive learned cognition must seek to avoid all blameworthy ignorance, and no other ignorance besides §.49.
blocks.meier-para-52: It is a ridiculous folly of many paltry minds among the learned when they credit their blameworthy ignorance to themselves as a merit, and, with Socrates, who possessed a very extensive learnedness, profess of themselves: that they know nothing, except that they know nothing.
blocks.meier-para-53: The more things someone cognizes in a learned manner, the more extensive is his learned cognition. A higher or noticeable, and consequently rarer, degree of the extensiveness of learned cognition is called polymathy (polyhistoria). It is undeniably a great perfection of learned cognition, provided one is not misled by greed for polyhistory 1) to transgress the limits of one's learned horizon, and 2) to neglect the remaining perfections of learned cognition all too noticeably.
blocks.meier-para-54: Whoever wants to make his learned cognition extensive enough must 1) learn many principal parts of learnedness. E.g. philosophy, theology, history, philology etc. 2) From each principal part many parts, e.g. from philosophy the doctrine of reason, metaphysics, physics, natural right etc. 3) Each of these parts he must again learn extensively, e.g. the doctrine of reason, and 4) of each single truth he must again seek to attain an extensive learned cognition, e.g. of the omniscience of God.
blocks.meier-para-55: An extensive learned cognition is thorough and complete (completa cognitio erudita) when it suffices for its aims, or when we cognize in a learned manner as much as the whole aim of our learned cognition requires. Extensiveness without thoroughness is not perfect enough, and one must accordingly learn to distinguish the principal truths from the side matters in every object of learned cognition, so that through the learned cognition of the former one may attain a complete learnedness.
blocks.meier-para-56: Whoever studies merely in a cavalier manner, in that he merely runs cursorily through an extensive outline of all parts of learnedness; goes through a very few parts of learnedness somewhat more extensively, but still quite briefly; and perhaps here and there investigates some particular matters because for some reason they especially please him: his learned cognition is a poor skeleton of learnedness, and deserves very little regard §.55.
blocks.meier-para-57: Because it is impossible for a human being to attain a thoroughly extensive learned cognition all at once; one must constantly seek to extend learned cognition: so that one does not go backward in it by failing to go further forward.
blocks.meier-para-58: Because, through the extension of learned cognition, the powers of cognition are at the same time made more capable; one need not fear that one will overload one's head through the constant extension of learned cognition, provided one does not in this occupation transgress the limits of the learned horizon.
blocks.meier-para-59: Although art is long and human life short, this consideration must rather incite us to learn as much as is possible with proper dispatch, than that it should instill in us a timidity and discouragement that hinders us from the extension of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-60: So that one may not regard the extension of learned cognition as unnecessary and useless, one must not set before oneself too small, trifling and base a purpose, which one strives to reach through one's learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-61: Since it is naturally necessary that we human beings forget much; for precisely this reason one must extend learned cognition very much, so that one may forget much and nonetheless still retain much. The truths that we forget have in any case not been wholly useless, because they have increased the degree of our powers of cognition.
blocks.meier-para-62: The extensiveness of learned cognition arises from a twofold source, both of which must be together: 1) from the extensiveness and rich content of the object, when it contains much in itself that can be cognized by a human being in a learned manner (vastitas obiectiva); and 2) from the extension of the powers of cognition (vastitas subiectiva), by virtue of which one is in a position to cognize much of a thing in a learned manner.
blocks.meier-para-63: Because it is impossible for a human being to learn all parts of learnedness in an equal degree of perfection; each must pick out one of them, with which he occupies himself most, and of which he strives to attain the most perfect learned cognition. This is his principal science (scientia eruditi principalis). Each must choose as his principal science that part of learnedness 1) which can be cognized by human beings in a very high degree of perfection, and 2) for which he possesses the most skill, rational inclination, and other means of furtherance.
blocks.meier-para-64: Each must 1) learn his principal science most extensively and thoroughly, and 2) investigate all other parts of learnedness in relation to his principal science. The more closely another part of learnedness is connected with the principal science, the more perfectly and extensively must one seek to cognize it in a learned manner §.63.
blocks.meier-para-65: The paltriness of learned cognition causes, among others, a threefold harm: 1) Learned pedantry and charlatanry (pedantismus et charlataneria eruditorum), by virtue of which one values far too highly the little that one understands, and despises everything else entirely; 2) a ridiculous conceit and a vain arrogance; and 3) little learnedness can make a human being unhappy for his whole life, in that he can fall into just such circumstances in which that which he has learned is not demanded of him, and that which he has not learned is expected of him. Of the magnitude of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-66: The magnitude of learned cognition requires not only a great object, but the cognition must also be great enough for the object §.26. The greater the object, and the more proportioned the cognition, the greater is the learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-67: The object of learned cognition is great considered in itself (magnitudo eruditae cognitionis obiectiva absoluta) when it contains much manifold in itself that can be cognized in a learned manner. For example: God, philosophy, history etc.
blocks.meier-para-68: The object of learned cognition is great with respect to its consequences (magnitudo eruditae cognitionis obiectiva respectiva), 1) when it is important (res digna, gravis), that is, when it has great consequences, e.g. when the happiness of human beings, the welfare of the fatherland etc. rests on it; 2) when it is fruitful (res foecunda), that is, when many consequences flow from it. E.g. godliness, for it is profitable for all things.
blocks.meier-para-69: Whoever wants to make his learned cognition truly great must seek to cognize nothing but absolutely great, important and fruitful things. The more the object contains in itself, the greater its consequences are, and the more consequences it has, the greater, more important and more fruitful it is; and the greater, more important and more fruitful is the learned cognition of it, insofar as one considers it, namely, with respect to its object.
blocks.meier-para-70: The magnitude of learned cognition that belongs to it itself (magnitudo cognitionis eruditae subiectiva) consists in this, when it is proportioned to the magnitude of its object §.66. The greater the object is, the more extensive, correct, distinct, certain and practical the learned cognition of it must be, and the more time and diligence must be expended on the attainment of it. The less great the object is, the less perfect the learned cognition must be, and the less time and diligence must be expended on the attainment of it.
blocks.meier-para-71: The imperfection of learned cognition that is opposed to its magnitude is called the smallness of it (parvitas, vilitas cognitionis eruditae); and it arises either from the smallness of the object, or from the learned cognition's not being proportioned to the object §.66.
blocks.meier-para-72: The object of learned cognition is small, considered in itself (parvitas cognitionis eruditae obiectiva absoluta), when it contains little in itself that can be cognized in a learned manner. E.g. the hairpins of Roman womenfolk.
blocks.meier-para-73: The object of learned cognition is small with respect to its consequences (parvitas cognitionis eruditae obiectiva respectiva), 1) when it is not important (res leviores), that is, when it has no great consequences, e.g. the doctrine of the composition of bodies from monads; 2) when it is unfruitful (res infoecunda, sterilis), that is, when it does not have many consequences, e.g. the doctrine of the incorporeality of the soul.
blocks.meier-para-74: When a thing is small in all respects §.72. 73, it is worth no learned cognition: for it is lowered beneath the horizon of it §.46. The less a thing contains in itself, the fewer and smaller consequences it has, the smaller it is. Among these trifles one must also count the vulgar and base things (res plebeiae, abiectae), the learned investigation of which would even be contrary to honorable morals, e.g. the outbreaks of vices among the rabble.
blocks.meier-para-75: The smallness of learned cognition that belongs to it itself (parvitas cognitionis eruditae subiectiva) consists in this, when it is not proportioned to the objects §.71. Consequently 1) when one seeks a more perfect learned cognition with more effort, and expends more time on it, than the object deserves; and 2) when one does not cognize an object as perfectly, does not investigate it with as much effort, and does not expend as much time on it as it deserves. E.g. whoever assails errors more learnedly and diligently than vices, his learned cognition is not proportioned enough.
blocks.meier-para-76: Whoever wants to make his learned cognition truly perfect must 1) if it is possible for him, choose for his principal science the greatest §.67. 68 part of learnedness §.63; 2) the greater a part of learnedness is, the more effort and diligence he must expend on it, and the more perfect the learned cognition of it must be; 3) the greater the truths are, the more effort and time he must expend on them, and the more perfect his learned cognition of them must be.
blocks.meier-para-77: Whoever possesses no mature and manly judgment cannot possibly judge of the true worth of things, and it is therefore impossible for him to attain the magnitude of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-78: Because all objects of learned cognition stand in a universal connection, they are all infinitely great, important and fruitful §.67. 68. An object is therefore called a trifle only in relation to us, because it is impossible for us to cognize its magnitude, importance and fruitfulness in a learned manner.
blocks.meier-para-79: Just as a learned cognition together with its object is not to be esteemed great because this or that small mind makes a great fuss about it; so one must also not hold it small because it is passed off by the same as a thing of little value.
blocks.meier-para-80: A learned cognition is not a trifle of little value and unfruitful because this or that dry and unfruitful head is not able to derive many and important consequences from it. The unfruitfulness of the soil is not to be imputed to the plant.
blocks.meier-para-81: The application of a great learned cognition to small, ridiculous, vulgar and contemptible cases can indeed accidentally make it ridiculous, contemptible and vulgar; but for that reason it must not be counted among the trifles of little value.
blocks.meier-para-82: When the great objects of learned cognition are represented and presented by this or that person in a contemptible and ridiculous manner; for that reason they must not be counted among the contemptible trifles.
blocks.meier-para-83: A scholar must not, through his own fault, through wretched application, and through ridiculous representations and expressions, make learned cognition ridiculous and contemptible §.81. 82.
blocks.meier-para-84: If a learned cognition should not be important and fruitful in our present circumstances, because we do not yet see its consequences; it can nevertheless become important and fruitful in the future, and it is therefore not a trifle on that account. We must also plant trees for our descendants, whose fruits we do not enjoy.
blocks.meier-para-85: One disgraces oneself if one does not hold abstract cognition, subtleties and profound distinctions to be great and important things, because they require much laborious reflection.
blocks.meier-para-86: The intermediate truths in an extensive doctrinal edifice indeed do not signify much in themselves; but because without them one cannot properly cognize the principal truths in a learned manner, they are for that reason great and worthy objects of our learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-87: A learned investigation is not important because it requires much effort, diligence and time, and because it cannot be undertaken without great learnedness: for there are also very difficult farces.
blocks.meier-para-88: A part of learnedness is not to be counted among the trifles because it is filled with many trifles.
blocks.meier-para-89: A learned cognition that is not great in one respect can be great in another respect, and it must therefore not be held to be a trifle §.67. 68. E.g. a cognition can be not important, but nevertheless fruitful.
blocks.meier-para-90: Because different scholars can have chosen different principal sciences §.63, a learned investigation can be great with respect to the one, and small with respect to the other.
blocks.meier-para-91: A great mind possesses the skill to have only a great learned cognition. His inclination toward it and his aversion to all trifles compel him always first to investigate the magnitude of the thing before he troubles himself to cognize it in a learned manner, so that he may know whether it is worth a learned cognition, and of what degree of perfection of it. Of the truth of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-92: A false or incorrect cognition (cognitio falsa) is a cognition that is no cognition and yet seems to be a cognition. A false learned cognition (cognitio erudita falsa) only seems to be a learned cognition, and it is either no cognition at all, or at least no learned cognition. E.g. those who assume the vegetative soul of plants, and derive the growth of plants from it, have a false learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-93: A true or correct cognition (cognitio vera) not only seems to be a cognition, but it is one in fact. A true learned cognition (cognitio erudita vera) not only seems to be a learned cognition, but it also deserves this name in fact. E.g. whoever demonstrates convincingly the actuality of God from the contingency of this world has a true learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-94: The marks of the correctness and incorrectness of cognition (criteria veritatis et falsitatis cognitionis) are the grounds from which it can be cognized that a cognition is true, or that it is false. And they are either present in the cognition itself, or not. The former are the internal, and the latter the external marks of correctness and incorrectness (criteria interna et externa veritatis et falsitatis cognitionis).
blocks.meier-para-95: The first internal mark of the truth of a cognition consists in its inner possibility (possibilitas cognitionis interna), insofar as it represents something possible, and contains nothing that is contrary to one another, even if one considers it quite alone. The internal impossibility of cognition (impossibilitas cognitionis interna), when it represents nothing, and when the manifold in it conflicts with one another, is therefore the first internal mark that it is false §.94.93. 92.
blocks.meier-para-96: The second internal mark of the truth of a cognition consists in this, when it is possible in a connection (possibilitas cognitionis hypothetica). Consequently 1) when it is a consequence of correct grounds, and 2) a ground of correct consequences, §.94. 93. A cognition is accordingly true when it is not impossible, and is in accordance with the principle of sufficient reason §.16.
blocks.meier-para-97: A cognition is false if it is impossible in connection (impossibilitas in nexu); consequently if it has no grounds or false grounds, and no consequences or false consequences §.96. And this is the other inner mark of its incorrectness §.94.
blocks.meier-para-98: We must not assume: 1) that a cognition is true because we do not become aware of any inner impossibility in it; 2) that it is false because we do not become aware of any inner possibility in it; 3) that a cognition is true whose groundlessness and false grounds and consequences we do not become aware of; 4) that a cognition is false of which we recognize no correct grounds and consequences. For we human beings are not omniscient.
blocks.meier-para-99: If we represent a thing to ourselves otherwise than it is, we believe that we cognize it, and yet do not cognize it. Our cognition is therefore false §.92. Moreover, all possible things have an inner possibility, grounds and consequences §.15.16. Logical truth of cognition (veritas cognitionis logica) therefore consists in its agreement with its object, and its logical incorrectness (falsitas cognitionis logica) in its not agreeing with its object §.95. 96. 97.
blocks.meier-para-100: If a cognition contains nothing true, it is wholly false (falsitas totalis), and if it contains nothing false, it is wholly true (veritas totalis). But it can be true and false at once, though in different respects (veritas et falsitas partialis). One must therefore not accept an extensive cognition wholly, because perhaps the greatest and most important part of it is true; and not reject it wholly, because perhaps the greatest and most important part of it is false. For example, the doctrinal systems of various religions.
blocks.meier-para-101: The more numerous and manifold the parts a cognition contains in itself that are possible together, the greater these parts are, and the more numerous and greater the correct grounds and consequences it has, the more correct the cognition is §.95. 96. Whoever, then, wants to improve his learned cognition as far as possible must seek to attain in it the greatest possible degree of truth.
blocks.meier-para-102: A cognition that is correct to a higher degree is called an exact cognition (cognitio exacta, exasciata); but one that is true to a lesser degree is called a coarse one (cognitio crassa). All coarse cognition must be avoided, and indeed all the more, the coarser it is, or the more and the more important falsehood it contains. Conversely, perfect learned cognition must be as exact as possible §.101, and the greater the objects are, the more exactly one must seek to cognize them §.70. The smaller they are, however, the less correct their cognition need be §.70.
blocks.meier-para-103: Learned cognition can be false in a threefold way: 1) when the cognition of the things is false, although the cognition of the grounds is correct; 2) when the cognition of the grounds is false, although the cognition of the things is correct; 3) when the representation of the connection between true grounds and consequences is incorrect §.100. A true learned cognition must therefore be a correct cognition of the things, of the grounds, and of their connection at the same time §.21.
blocks.meier-para-104: By truths (veritates) one also understands true cognition itself, and then all truths are either dogmatic (veritates dogmaticae) or historical (veritates historicae). The former can and must be cognized from the inner marks of truth, the latter only from the outer ones. E.g., that there is a GOD is a dogmatic truth; but that David was the second king of the Israelites is a historical one. A doctrinal system (systema) is a multitude of dogmatic truths that are connected with one another in such a way that, taken together, they make up one cognition that one can consider as a whole.
blocks.meier-para-105: The more truths occur in a doctrinal system, and the greater and more correct they are, the more perfect it is §.104. For the most exact truth of a doctrinal system it is required: 1) that all its parts are most exactly correct; 2) that none contradicts another; and 3) that they are all connected, in that each is either a ground of the rest, or a consequence, or both at the same time §.95. 96. Since there is no truth outside doctrinal systems §.96. 104, learned cognition must be systematic if it is to be perfectly correct at all.
blocks.meier-para-106: All truths are either merely aesthetic truths (veritates mere aestheticae), which must be cognized merely beautifully, and with these learned cognition must never occupy itself; or merely learned (veritates mere eruditae), which can only be cognized in a learned way, and with these alone learned cognition must not occupy itself, for it would otherwise be merely learned §.32; or both at once (veritates aesthetico-eruditae), and these are the foremost object of a truly perfect learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-107: Since truth is not the only perfection of learned cognition, a scholar can never be excused if he occupies himself with a learned investigation merely because it is true. It is not good to think and to say all truths.
blocks.meier-para-108: Everyone must seek to cognize his principal science most exactly §.102, and in the highest possible degree systematically §.105 §.63.
blocks.meier-para-109: Error (cognitio erronea, error) consists in our holding false cognition to be true, and true cognition to be false. Consequently 1) every erroneous cognition is false §.99; 2) not every false cognition is erroneous, namely when we recognize that it is false §.99; 3) error arises from false cognition. If we had no false cognition at all, we could also have no errors. Error is worse than merely false cognition, for it is a hidden poison. Learned cognition can therefore be erroneous in a threefold way §.103.
blocks.meier-para-110: If we transgress the rules of the 98th paragraph, error arises §.109. The first source of all errors is therefore ignorance §.41, when it is joined by precipitancy, by virtue of which we deny that of which we have no cognition.
blocks.meier-para-111: Error is either an avoidable one (error vincibilis) or an unavoidable one (error invincibilis). The former arises from an avoidable, the latter from an unavoidable ignorance §.43. The former is only a blameworthy stain on learned cognition, but the latter can and may not be avoided.
blocks.meier-para-112: The more extensive, important and fruitful an error is, and the more easily it could have been prevented, the greater it is. The greater an error is, the more it disgraces learned cognition, and the more carefully it must be prevented. Consequently everyone must seek especially to prevent the errors in his principal science §.108.
blocks.meier-para-113: A cognition is manifestly false (cognitio aperte falsa) if its incorrectness is discovered merely by considering it, e.g., a square triangle. But if one must undertake a more extensive investigation in order to discover its incorrectness, it is falsely concealed (cognitio cuius falsitas latet), e.g., matter can think. An error by which a manifestly false cognition is accepted as true is an absurd, nonsensical and stupid error (cognitio absurda, absona). Not all errors are absurdities.
blocks.meier-para-114: All truths are either absolutely necessary (veritates absolute necessariae) or contingent truths (veritates contingentes). In the former it is wholly impossible that they should be false, e.g., there is a GOD. The latter, however, could also be false, e.g., this world is actual. Since error is easier to avoid in the former, it is greater than error in contingent truths §.112. On the clarity of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-115: A mark, a characteristic of cognition and of things (nota, character cognitionis et rei) is that in the cognition or in the things which, when it is cognized, is the ground why we are conscious of them; or they are the distinguishing parts of cognition and of its objects. Where there is consciousness, therefore, marks are cognized §.13. E.g., reason is a mark of the human being, and of the cognition we have of him.
blocks.meier-para-116: Marks in turn have their marks §.115. Consequently all marks of a thing are either immediate marks (notae immediatae, proximae) or mediate ones (notae mediatae, remotae). The latter are marks of marks, the former only marks of the thing, though they are not marks of its marks. E.g., reason is an immediate mark of the human being, but because reason is a faculty of distinctly understanding the connection of things, the faculty is a mediate mark of the human being. Consciousness rests on the immediate marks §.13.
blocks.meier-para-117: Marks are either negative (notae negativae) or affirmative (notae affirmativae, positivae). Through the former we represent something to ourselves as absent in the thing, and thereby we cognize only what it is not; e.g., the unreason of unreasoning animals. Through the latter we represent something to ourselves as present in the thing, and through them we cognize what the thing is, e.g., the reason of human beings. Although both kinds can cause consciousness, the affirmative are nevertheless better marks than the negative.
blocks.meier-para-118: Marks are either more weighty (notae graviores) or lesser marks (notae leviores). The former reveal a greater, the latter a lesser difference of the thing. Either fruitful (notae foecundae) or unfruitful marks (notae infoecundae). The former reveal a manifold difference from many things, the latter do not. Reason is a weighty and fruitful mark of a human being; but that he is a thing is a lesser and more unfruitful one. The more weighty and fruitful the marks are, therefore, the more they promote consciousness.
blocks.meier-para-119: Since marks are grounds §.115, they are either sufficient grounds of consciousness or insufficient grounds §.15. The former are sufficient (notae sufficientes), and the latter insufficient marks (notae insufficientes). The former are better marks than the latter. The faculty of thinking is an insufficient mark of a spirit; but that it has understanding, a sufficient one.
blocks.meier-para-120: Marks are either absolutely necessary and unchangeable (notae absolute necessariae et invariabiles) or contingent and changeable marks (notae contingentes et variabiles). The former are constituted so that without them the thing cannot be represented, e.g., the reason of the human being; the latter, however, are constituted so that without them the thing can nevertheless be represented, e.g., the actual thinking of the human being. The former are better marks than the latter.
blocks.meier-para-121: Marks can be represented in a thing either without considering it in connection with other things outside it, or not. The latter are outer marks or relations (notae externae, relationes), e.g., the dominion of a human being. The former are inner marks (notae internae). The latter are either necessary or contingent §.120. The contingent ones are called contingent constitutions (modi), e.g., the learning of a human being. The necessary ones are either the grounds of all the remaining determinations, or not. The latter are the attributes (attributa), e.g., the faculty of thinking in a human being. The former are called the essential parts (essentialia), e.g., the reason of the human being. The sum total of all essential parts is the essence (essentia).
blocks.meier-para-122: The more marks we cognize of a thing, the greater these marks are, and the more perfectly we cognize the marks, the greater and better the consciousness is §.13. Consequently the affirmative, weighty, fruitful, inner, necessary and sufficient marks cause a greater and better consciousness than those opposed to them §.117-121.
blocks.meier-para-123: A representation, insofar as we are conscious of it, is called a thought (cogitatio). Consequently not every representation and cognition is a thought. And what has been proved of consciousness also holds of thinking §.115.116. 122.
blocks.meier-para-124: A cognition contains either as many marks as are required for consciousness, or not. The former is a clear cognition (cognitio clara), which is one and the same with the thought, and with the cognition of which we are conscious §.123. The latter is an obscure cognition (cognitio obscura), which is therefore neither a thought nor connected with consciousness §.123. The former is more perfect than the latter. When we cannot recall a word, and yet it seems as if it were running around on the tip of our tongue, then we have an obscure representation of it.
blocks.meier-para-125: Obscure cognition is either absolutely obscure (cognitio absolute obscura) or relatively so (cognitio relative obscura). The former would have to be so obscure that it would be absolutely impossible to make it clear. No true cognition is absolutely obscure, and one must therefore hold nothing to be absolutely obscure. All true obscure cognition is only relatively obscure, that is, the powers of this or that thinking being are not sufficient to make it clear. And then either the object is chiefly to blame for this obscurity, or the human being to whom the cognition is obscure. The former is the obscurity of the things (cognitio obiective obscura), and the latter the obscurity in the head of him to whom the cognition is so obscure (cognitio subiective obscura). E.g., things that are too far removed from us, or too small, are to blame that we sense them obscurely. But whoever finds logic obscure is himself to blame for it. Finally, an obscure cognition is either wholly obscure (cognitio totaliter obscura), when we are not at all conscious of it, or obscure only in part (cognitio partialiter obscura), when we are conscious and also not conscious of it at the same time. All our clear cognition is always partly obscure to us, because we are not capable of thoroughly thinking through a single thing completely.
blocks.meier-para-126: One human being can cognize what another does not cognize, and one can therefore cognize marks that are unknown to the other §.115. Consequently one can cognize clearly what the other cognizes only obscurely §.124. One must therefore not infer: 1) what is clear to me is also clear to others; 2) what is obscure to me is also obscure to others; 3) what is clear to me now will also be clear to me in the future; 4) what is obscure to me now will also remain obscure to me in the future.
blocks.meier-para-127: The more marks that are required for consciousness are unknown to us, and the greater the marks that are unknown to us, and the more force is required to make a cognition clear, the greater its obscurity is. Before a cognition can become clear, therefore, one must often expend much time and effort to diminish its obscurity.
blocks.meier-para-128: Because we have much clear cognition whose marks we do cognize §.115, but not clearly, there are actually obscure representations present in our soul, which make up the materials from which the soul gradually composes its clear cognition.
blocks.meier-para-129: The obscurity of cognition arises from a threefold source: 1) when a human being does not possess sufficient powers to make it clear. This lack of powers is either necessary or not, and in the latter case the human being should either have acquired the powers or not; 2) from the lack of attention, which arises either from a necessary lack of powers, or because we may not pay attention to a certain cognition, or because we do not pay attention to it although we should; 3) from ignorance of such things without which a certain cognition cannot become clear, whether this ignorance be necessary or contingent, praiseworthy or blameworthy §.43.50. 51. All obscurity of cognition is therefore either necessary or contingent, praiseworthy or blameworthy. Consequently, in the improvement of cognition one must seek to avoid only the contingent and blameworthy obscurity; and the obscurity that is necessary and praiseworthy in one person can be contingent and blameworthy in another.
blocks.meier-para-130: Obscure cognition 1) can be true, but it can also be false §.92.93. Not every obscure cognition is therefore false; 2) is no learned cognition, insofar as it is obscure. It is an unavoidable evil in the learned cognition of human beings.
blocks.meier-para-131: The action by which the obscurity of cognition is diminished, and the clarity of cognition is produced and increased, is called the unfolding or development of cognition (evolutio, explanatio cognitionis), just as the opposed action is called its enfolding (cognitionis involutio). For the former, a) three things are required beforehand: 1) one investigates as far as possible whether the obscurity of the cognition one wants to develop is necessary or contingent, unculpable or culpable. In the latter case we may only venture the development. 2) One investigates whether the development of it belongs to the horizon of our clear cognition or not. In the former case this work is alone permitted to us. 3) One investigates whether this development does not presuppose some other clear cognition, without which it cannot take place. And if this matter is in fact so, one must not undertake this work until we have obtained this other clear cognition §.129. b) For the unfolding itself, three things are required: 1) one directs one's attention to the thing one wants to cognize clearly; 2) one compares it with other things different from it, so that one may cognize its marks §.115; 3) one abstracts from all other things, or one obscures them, in that one pays attention to the object. The more often, more strongly and longer one pays attention to a thing, the more things one compares it with, the more strongly one abstracts from other things, the better and sooner the cognition of it develops, even if one should at first perform this work in vain several times.
blocks.meier-para-132: Through a clear cognition we are either capable of distinguishing the object constantly and in all circumstances from all possible other things, or not. In the first case our cognition is completely clear (cognitio complete clara), e.g., the representation of the color red; in the second, however, incompletely clear (cognitio incomplete clara), e.g., when we do indeed taste that a wine is Rhine wine, but cannot taste of what sort it is. The former is more perfect than the latter, because the latter contains more obscurity than the former §.124, and we attain it through the cognition of the necessary, unchangeable and sufficient marks §.119. 120. 121.
blocks.meier-para-133: If we have a clear cognition, we are either conscious of everything that is found in the object, or not. If the first, the cognition is wholly clear (cognitio totaliter clara). If the latter, it is clear only in part (cognitio partialiter clara). No human clear cognition is wholly clear §.125, and a cognition can be completely clear although it is not wholly clear §.132. Meanwhile a cognition is all the more perfect, the more its clarity approaches total clarity §.124.
blocks.meier-para-134: The more marks we cognize, consequently from the more numerous and more similar things we can distinguish a thing; the greater the marks, and the better we cognize all the marks; the more easily we can be conscious of a cognition and of its object: the clearer our cognition is §.124, and thus also the more perfect. In the improvement of a cognition, therefore, one must seek to attain the highest possible degree of its clarity.
blocks.meier-para-135: A cognition that is clearer through the multitude of marks is called a lively cognition (cognitio extensive clarior, vivida); e.g., the melodious song of the nightingale runs resounding through the valleys. But one that is clearer through the greatness of the marks and their clearer representation is clearer in intensity (cognitio intensive clarior). Only logic occupies itself with the latter degree of clarity §.1. 17. 21.
blocks.meier-para-136: If we forget marks of a clear cognition, a clearer cognition can be changed into a less clear one, and finally into a wholly obscure cognition §.124. Whoever wants to prevent the enfolding of clear cognition §.131 must therefore prevent forgetting.
blocks.meier-para-137: A cognition considered with regard to the intensity of clarity is either distinct or confused §.14. 135. In the former the marks are also clear, in the latter, however, obscure §.14. 115. 124. Since distinctness is therefore a manifold clarity, distinct cognition is more perfect than confused §.124.
blocks.meier-para-138: Since all learned cognition is distinct §.21. 17, confused cognition, insofar as it is confused, is not learned §.137. Just as the beautiful sciences therefore occupy themselves with improving the confused half of human cognition, so a scholar must improve its distinct half through logic. Obscurity and confusion are a necessary evil in learned cognition, which one either also seeks to improve incidentally or not. In the latter case a merely learned cognition arises, and in the former a learned cognition that is at the same time beautiful §.24.
blocks.meier-para-139: The action by which a certain degree of distinctness is produced in our cognition is called the resolution of cognition (resolutio, analysis, anatomia cognitionis). A cognition can be resolved if it can be made distinct by some thinking being (cognitio resolubilis). Insofar as it cannot become distinct, however, it is a cognition that cannot be resolved (cognitio irresolubilis). And then it is either wholly and utterly impossible that it become distinct, or it cannot become distinct only through the powers of this or that thinking being. If the first, it cannot be resolved absolutely (cognitio absolute irresolubilis). If the latter, it cannot be resolved only relatively (cognitio respective irresolubilis). If a true cognition could not be resolved absolutely, its marks would have to be absolutely obscure §.137. Since this is impossible §.120, all true cognition that cannot be resolved is so constituted only relatively.
blocks.meier-para-140: Insofar as we have a distinct cognition of a thing, we comprehend it (concipere). What can be cognized distinctly is comprehensible (conceptibile). What cannot be cognized distinctly is incomprehensible (inconceptibile), either absolutely (absolute inconceptibile), if it cannot be resolved absolutely; or only relatively (relative inconceptibile), if it cannot be resolved relatively. All possible things are incomprehensible only relatively §.139, and what we cognize in a learned way, we comprehend always insofar §.21.17.
blocks.meier-para-141: What we do not comprehend is not on that account an absurd thing §.140. And since a cognition can be distinct to one human being that is confused or even obscure to another §.126, one must not infer: what we do not comprehend, others do not comprehend either; what we comprehend, others comprehend; what I now comprehend, I shall also comprehend in the future; what I do not now comprehend, I shall also not comprehend in the future. These inferences hold also when the talk is of mere possibility or impossibility.
blocks.meier-para-142: If one wants to resolve a cognition, one must 1) develop it §.131, if it should not already be clear in us beforehand. 2) One must think through the clear cognition, or develop its marks gradually, according to §.131. The more marks, and the better marks §.116-121 one develops, the better it is. 3) One reflects on the developed marks, or one represents them together as One cognition; otherwise we would think the object only piecemeal, and that is not yet a distinct cognition of the whole object. 4) One represents the developed marks to oneself in the same connection and in the same order as they are found in the object. Otherwise the distinct cognition does not agree with the object, and all disorder puts us into confusion. 5) One must obscure, or abstract from, all other things and representations that have not been drawn into reflection, so that the cognition does not at once become confused again.
blocks.meier-para-143: The more and greater clear marks we cognize of a thing, the better we cognize the marks, consequently the more extensive, proportioned, correct, clearer, certain and practical: the more distinct the cognition is §.137.25-30.
blocks.meier-para-144: A distinct cognition is either wholly distinct (cognitio totaliter distincta) or distinct only in part (cognitio partialiter distincta). The former contains no obscurity and confusion at all, the latter, however, contains such. No human distinct cognition is wholly distinct §.133. But it is all the more distinct, the nearer its distinctness comes to total distinctness § 142.
blocks.meier-para-145: The confusion of cognition arises, 1) from the sources of obscurity, for it consists in the obscurity of the marks §.137. 129. 2) From the necessary or contingent, praiseworthy or blameworthy lack of reflection; likewise 3) of deliberation; 4) from the lack of order in thinking, and 5) from a necessary or contingent, praiseworthy or blameworthy lack of abstraction §.142.
blocks.meier-para-146: There is therefore not only a confusion in all our cognition that we absolutely cannot prevent; but there is also a confusion that we could prevent, but we may not, because it is found beneath or outside our horizon §.146. Before we venture upon the resolution of a cognition, therefore, we must investigate beforehand as far as possible whether we can or may perform it.
blocks.meier-para-147: The marks of a distinct cognition are clear §.137. They are therefore either distinct or confused §.137. In the first case we have an adequate cognition (cognitio adaequata), in the other, however, an inadequate one (cognitio inadaequata), e.g., vice is an acquired skill in sinning. An acquired skill is a facility in acting that we have obtained through practice, and we sin when we undertake evil free actions. This is an adequate cognition of vice, but it would be inadequate if I had no distinct cognition of skill and of sin. Adequacy is a manifold distinctness, and thus a perfection of cognition §.137. Inadequacy consists in the confusion of the cognition of the marks, and thus arises from the sources of confusion in general §.145. The more distinct marks a cognition contains, and the more distinct they are, the more adequate the cognition is. And the most perfect learned cognition must be as adequate as possible §.21.
blocks.meier-para-148: Adequacy arises from the resolution of the marks §.147. 142. The more remote the marks are that we resolve in turn, the more adequate the cognition becomes §.116. 147. A higher degree of adequacy is a profound cognition (cognitio profunda, purior). And in resolving a cognition, we bring this business to an end when we discover the marks that we cannot resolve further. But we stop in the resolution when we do not resolve further marks that we nevertheless could resolve. Since it would be a loathsome labor if we wanted always to bring the resolution of all our distinct cognition to an end; we must always have a reasonable purpose for which we resolve a cognition, and as soon as we have attained it, we must interrupt this work for the time being. It is in any case impossible for a human being to avoid all inadequacy in his cognition §.144.
blocks.meier-para-149: Distinct cognition is either completely distinct (cognitio complete distincta) or incompletely so (cognitio incomplete distincta) §.132. The former is more perfect than the latter §.132. E.g., if I represent to myself a spirit as a being that can think, I have a distinct but incomplete cognition of it. But if I represent it to myself as a thing that has understanding, my distinct cognition of a spirit is at the same time complete.
blocks.meier-para-150: If one wants to make a distinct cognition of a thing complete, one must 1) seek to discover those marks that are found outside it in no other thing; or 2) one must discover so many marks as, taken together, belong to no other thing. E.g., virtue is a skill of free lawful actions. Although each of these marks is also found in things that are not virtues, they are nevertheless, taken together, found in no other thing. And the sum total of these four marks therefore makes the distinct representation of virtue a completely distinct representation.
blocks.meier-para-151: A distinct cognition is either a determinate cognition (cognitio determinata) or an indeterminate cognition (cognitio indeterminata). The former is completely distinct, and contains not a single mark more than is absolutely necessary for completeness. E.g., a spirit is a being that has understanding. The latter contains either too few marks, and that is the incompletely distinct cognition §.149; or it contains more clear marks than are necessary for completeness, and that is an all too prolix cognition (cognitio nimis prolixa). E.g., a spirit is a thinking being that possesses understanding and free will. If one therefore separates from a completely distinct cognition those marks that are either not necessary for completeness or that follow from other marks of the same cognition, it becomes determinate. Determination is only a perfection of merely learned cognition §.24, when one wants to make the comprehension of a thing easier for the weak, profound understanding of the human being.
blocks.meier-para-152: The most adequate cognition can gradually become less adequate, inadequate, confused, and finally wholly obscure, if, on account of forgetting, the clear cognition becomes obscure §.136. Whoever wants to prevent this loss of perfections must therefore seek to prevent forgetting. We human beings are never wholly secure in the possession of our perfections, and we must therefore be diligently on our guard everywhere.
blocks.meier-para-153: Whoever wants to make learned cognition truly perfect with regard to its clarity must proportion the degree of clarity to the greatness of the objects §.70. Consequently, the more extensive and greater the object is, the more numerous, better and greater the kinds and degrees of clarity by which the learned cognition of it must be illuminated. In the opposite case one must also behave oppositely in this matter.
blocks.meier-para-154: Every scholar must, if it is otherwise possible for him, choose for his principal science that part of learning which is capable of the most manifold and greatest clarity; and everyone must seek to attain in his principal science the very clearest cognition §.63. 64. He must therefore be a bright head, or prefer the clearest truths, and constantly think as clearly as possible. A dark head scarcely deserves the name of a scholar. On the certainty of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-155: Certainty (certitudo subiective spectata) is the consciousness of truth, or the clear cognition of truth §.29. If one wants to possess a certain learned cognition, therefore, it must be true according to the rules of the fourth section, and clear in the proper way according to the rules of the fifth section.
blocks.meier-para-156: If we cognize clearly neither that something is true nor that it is false, our cognition of it is uncertain (incertitudo). Uncertainty is therefore to be found only as an imperfection in our cognition. A cognition that is not uncertain to us is either certainly true (certo vera cognitio), when we are conscious of its truth, or certainly false (certo falsa cognitio), when we are conscious of its incorrectness §.155.
blocks.meier-para-157: All certainty is either a distinct or a confused cognition of truth §.155. 137. The latter is sensitive certainty (certitudo sensitiva), and when it is perfect to a higher degree, aesthetic (certitudo aesthetica). The former is rational certainty (certitudo rationalis), and when it is perfect to a higher degree, it is called logical or learned (certitudo logica, erudita). No human certain cognition can be merely rational and learned §.144.
blocks.meier-para-158: Rational certainty is either an adequate certainty (certitudo adaequata), when we are in turn rationally certain of the marks of truth; or an inadequate one (certitudo inadaequata), when we are only sensitively certain of the marks of truth §.157. 147. E.g., what thinks, is actual; I think, therefore I am actual. Because I have a distinct certainty of the first proposition, I am insofar adequately certain of the last proposition. But because the second proposition is only sensitively certain to me, the last proposition is insofar only inadequately certain to me.
blocks.meier-para-159: Certainty is either a complete one (completa certitudo) or an incomplete certainty (incompleta certitudo) §.132.149. Determinate certainty (certitudo determinata) is a complete certainty that contains no more marks of truth than are indispensable for complete certainty §.151.
blocks.meier-para-160: Through complete certainty the mind is always so calmed that it is raised above all reasonable fear of the opposite; incomplete certainty, however, cannot wholly drive out this reasonable fear §.159. Meanwhile a human being can often be freed from all fear of the opposite, and nevertheless not even be certain in general.
blocks.meier-para-161: Determinate certainty, if it is moreover as adequate as possible, is mathematical certainty (certitudo mathematica).
blocks.meier-para-162: We have a total certainty of a thing (certitudo totalis) if everything we cognize of it is certain to us; but if not all of this is certain to us, the thing is certain to us only in part (certitudo partialis).
blocks.meier-para-163: A certain cognition is called, 1) convincing (cognitio convincens), insofar as it is completely certain, and the production of such a certain cognition is called conviction (convictio); 2) undeniable (cognitio evidens, indubitata), insofar as we cognize clearly that that of which we are convinced could not possibly be false; 3) thorough (cognitio solida), insofar as the certainty is adequate; or also when it is as great and of the kind as is required.
blocks.meier-para-164: The more things we cognize with certainty, and the more we cognize with certainty of each object; the greater the things are that we cognize with certainty, and the more clearly we cognize the truth: the greater the certainty is §.155. Whoever wants to improve learned cognition properly must therefore make it as certain as is possible, in that he produces certainty of all kinds, and in each kind the greatest degree of certainty, as far as, namely, the remaining rules of the perfection of learned cognition permit.
blocks.meier-para-165: We must not infer: 1) What is certain to me is also certain to other people, and conversely §.126. 2) What is uncertain to me is, considered in itself, uncertain, or even false §.156. 3) What is uncertain to me is also uncertain to other people, and conversely §.126. 4) What is certain to me now will always remain certain to me in the future §.126. 5) What is uncertain to me now will always remain uncertain to me in the future §.126. 6) If not everything in an object is certain, it has no certainty at all §.162.
blocks.meier-para-166: Because we attain some kinds of certainty, especially of logical certainty, only gradually, one must on the one hand not become vexed if certainty will not follow as quickly as we sometimes wish; on the other hand one must be distrustful if we have in some case become certain all too quickly, whether one may not have overlooked something. In the attainment of certainty one must hasten slowly.
blocks.meier-para-167: If a cognition is not certain in the kind and to the degree that it could and should be, it is called a shallow cognition (cognitio superficiaria).
blocks.meier-para-168: We give a cognition our assent, or we accept it (assentiri, ponere aliquid), when we hold it to be true; we reject it (tollere aliquid), when we hold it to be false; and we withhold our assent (suspendere iudicium), when we do neither of the two. When we accept or reject an uncertain cognition, we do this either because we recognize some marks of correctness or incorrectness, or we recognize none of these marks at all. In the latter case we are precipitate (praecipitantia), and the uncertain cognition that we accept or reject out of precipitancy is a begged cognition, a prejudice, a preconceived opinion (praecaria cognitio, praeiudicium, praeconcepta opinio). Begged cognition is no learned cognition at all §.21. 17, and all prejudices can be avoided in learned cognition, and they are therefore an unjustifiable stain upon it.
blocks.meier-para-169: Because the correctness and incorrectness of things does not depend on our insights, 1) that which we accept through a prejudice can be false, and that which we reject through a prejudice can be true. 2) That which we accept through a prejudice can in fact be true, and that which we reject through a prejudice can actually be false. 3) In every prejudice there is always something erroneous and false, because we believe ourselves to be certain when we are nevertheless not certain §.168.
blocks.meier-para-170: A logical prejudice (praeiudicium logicum) is a prejudice by which the perfection of learned cognition, especially its thoroughness, is hindered. For example: a) the prejudice of excessively great confidence (praeiudicium nimiae confidentiae), when one hastily holds something to be logically perfect. 1) The prejudice of excessively great authority (praeiudicium autoritatis), when we accept or reject something because a person accepts and rejects it whom we honor so highly that we hold him worthy of imitation. 2) Logical egoism (egoismus logicus), when someone holds something to be logically perfect because he himself is its author. 3) The prejudice of antiquity (praeiudicium antiquitatis), when we hold something to be true because it is an old opinion. 4) The prejudice of novelty (praeiudicium novitatis), when we hold something to be true because it is a new opinion. 5) The prejudice of the accepted system of doctrine (praeiudicium systematis), when one accepts something merely because it conforms to our system of doctrine, and rejects it because it is contrary to it. 6) The prejudice of lazy trust (praeiudicium pigritiae), when one believes that with less diligence one can get just as far in learned cognition as with greater. 7) The prejudice of shallowness (praeiudicium corticis), when one believes that with a shallow cognition one can get just as far as with a thorough one. b) The prejudice of excessively great distrust (praeiudicium nimiae diffidentiae), when one hastily holds something to be logically imperfect. 1) The prejudice of antiquity (praeiudicium antiquitatis), when one rejects something because it is old. 2) The prejudice of novelty (praeiudicium novitatis), when one rejects something because it is new. 3) The prejudice of nationality (nazarethismus), when one rejects something because it stems from a certain people. 4) The prejudice of the distrust which one places in oneself (praeiudicium nimiae diffidentiae in se ipsum positae), when one trusts oneself too little, etc.
blocks.meier-para-171: When we accept or reject an uncertain cognition on account of some marks of correctness and incorrectness, §.168, we either recognize more and stronger grounds for accepting it than for rejecting it, and then our cognition is probable (cognitio probabilis, verosimilis); or we recognize more and stronger grounds for rejecting it than for accepting it, and so we have an improbable cognition (cognitio improbabilis); or the grounds on both sides are equal to one another, and then it is a doubtful cognition (cognitio dubia). E.g. It is probable that the planets are inhabited, but it is improbable that the sun is. As often as we cannot arrive at any resolution, so often we have a doubtful cognition.
blocks.meier-para-172: Because human beings differ so infinitely from one another in their cognition, one can accept or reject through a prejudice a thing which another holds to be quite certainly true, a third quite certainly false, a fourth probable, a fifth improbable, and a sixth doubtful. The first always acts wrongly. The two following cannot possibly both be right or both be wrong. The last three, however, can all be right together §.159. 168. 171.
blocks.meier-para-173: Probability, improbability and doubtfulness are uncertainties §.171, and thus are not to be found in the objects of our cognition §.156. The most probable things can be false, and the most improbable true.
blocks.meier-para-174: Prejudices one must hold neither true nor false §.168, just as with doubtful cognition §.171. Improbable cognition one must hold false, and probable cognition true, yet both under a constant fear of the opposite §.171. To exhaustively certain cognition we must give our assent with the greatest confidence, without fearing the opposite §.159.
blocks.meier-para-175: The more and greater grounds we recognize for accepting something, the fewer and smaller grounds we recognize for rejecting it, the better we recognize the former and the worse the latter: the greater is the probability, and the greater the improbability of the opposite §.171. A degree of probability so great that it is as good in our regular conduct as an exhaustive certainty is called moral certainty (certitudo moralis).
blocks.meier-para-176: When we hold something to be true or false, any cognition of a ground for the opposite is called a doubt (dubium). Doubts are cognized either in a merely obscure and indistinct way, or in a rational and learned manner. The former are called scruples (scrupulus), and the latter objections (obiectio).
