blocks.meier-para-177: All doubts are either true doubts (dubium verum), or false ones (dubium falsum) §.176. 92. 93, which, if they seem to be true, have a great semblance. When one clearly recognizes what is incorrect in a false doubt, the doubt is resolved or answered (dubium resolvitur, seu ad dubium respondetur). All doubts are either answerable or unanswerable, and both either absolutely or relatively (dubium absolute et respective resolubile aut irresolubile). Consequently 1) doubts can be raised against all truths, and nothing is false because doubts are raised against it; 2) against a truth doubts can be raised that are unanswerable to this or that person; 3) against no truth can absolutely unanswerable doubts be raised. Established truths (veritates indubitatae, extra omnem dubitationis aleam positae) are either such truths as are exhaustively certain; or against which no other doubts can be raised than those that are answerable and have already been answered. Truths that are not established are unestablished truths (veritates non indubitatae).
blocks.meier-para-178: For full conviction of a truth 1) it is not required that the unknown doubts against it be answered; nor 2) that the scruples be answered, for they deserve no answer at all; 3) nor that all known doubts be answered; there can even be among them some which are unanswerable to a person, and who nevertheless can be fully convinced; 4) it is required that all doubts which make the mind waver be answered; 5) the answering of doubts always contributes to the increase of certainty, and to the strengthening of conviction §.176.
blocks.meier-para-179: The uncertainty of cognition arises 1) from the limitation of our power of cognition, for which we are either to blame or not to blame; 2) from the lack of proper attention, reflection, diligence and patience §.129. 145, which can be either necessary or contingent, blameworthy or praiseworthy; 3) from a necessary or contingent, praiseworthy or blameworthy ignorance of such truths without whose cognition another truth cannot become certain to us § 43. 50. 51; 4) from excessively strong attention to the doubts §.176.
blocks.meier-para-180: In human cognition there is an uncertainty 1) which is wholly unavoidable, and which redounds neither to our shame nor to our honor; 2) which we need not avoid, even if we could, because its object is found outside our horizon, or beneath it, and which redounds to a person's honor; 3) which a person can and should avoid, because the opposite certainty belongs within his horizon §.178. This last always redounds to our shame, and whoever wants to improve his learned cognition as far as possible must seek to avoid all uncertainty of the third kind.
blocks.meier-para-181: An opinion (opinio) is any uncertain cognition, insofar as we accept it and at the same time recognize that it is not certain. An opinion is either accepted as a ground from which we explain the appearances in the world, or not. The latter is a common opinion (opinio vulgaris). The former is a philosophical or learned opinion (hypothesis philosophica, erudita), e.g. when one assumes the efflux of a magnetic matter in order to explain thereby how the magnet attracts iron.
blocks.meier-para-182: All opinions 1) have the nature of all uncertain cognition; 2) common opinions are, at least in learned cognition, wholly to be despised; 3) what is an opinion to some is not an opinion to all; 4) one must not make too much of learned opinions, for they belong to the more imperfect half of learned cognition; 5) one must not wholly despise them, because they are the transition from historical cognition to fully certain learned cognition §.181.
blocks.meier-para-183: In the case of learned opinions one must observe the following rules: 1) one must hold no learned opinion to be certainly true, and must not show as much zeal for it as for certain truths. 2) One must accept them only in case of necessity, when we cannot yet have any better learned cognition. 3) One must accept no manifestly false opinion, which is either internally impossible, or contradicts another undeniable truth, or contradicts the appearances. An appearance does not contradict an opinion merely because we cannot derive it from it. 4) One must be ready to let go of the most elegant and most learned opinion as soon as one discovers its incorrectness. 5) One must not accept a learned opinion before one has brought it to some probability. One must therefore, among other things, be able to explain most of the appearances from it. 6) One must constantly endeavor to transform an opinion into a certain cognition. 7) One must have no excessively great inclination toward opinions, and not invent too many of them. 8) One must not hold an opinion to be true because it is new, pleasing, marvelous, harmless, edifying, and required much effort, learning, wit and acuteness before it was invented.
blocks.meier-para-184: Certainty and conviction are either true or merely apparent. The error through which we imagine ourselves to be convinced, when we are nevertheless not convinced, is called persuasion in the bad sense (persuasio malo significatu). Since through it the certainty of learned cognition is hindered, one must seek to prevent it as far as possible. It arises, however: 1) from ignorance of the rules of logic; 2) from the lack of a certain cognition, for then one does not yet know how it feels with a true conviction; 3) from prejudices §.169. 170. 171; 4) from excessive negligence and haste. Insofar as it lies within a person's power to remove these causes of persuasion, so far is he also able to avoid this fault himself.
blocks.meier-para-185: When one now prevents persuasion and attains a thorough conviction, one acquires a science (scientia subiective spectata), that is, a learned cognition insofar as it is exhaustively certain.
blocks.meier-para-186: The greater, more important and more fruitful the object of our learned cognition is, the more certain our cognition must be §.70; that is, we must seek to make the cognition of it thorough according to the most and best kinds of certainty, and in the highest degrees of it. With smaller objects the matter stands exactly the reverse.
blocks.meier-para-187: Each person must not only choose for his principal science that part of learning which is capable of the greatest certainty, so far as is otherwise possible for him; but he must also seek to raise his chosen principal science to the highest possible degree of certainty §.63.64.
blocks.meier-para-188: Exhaustive certainty consists in the consciousness of truth §.155, consequently that it is possible and grounded §.94.96, so that no fear of the opposite remains §.160. Consequently we are then conscious that the opposite is false, impossible and groundless §.95. 97. Consequently exhaustive certainty arises from the consciousness of the necessity of truth §.114.
blocks.meier-para-189: Exhaustive certainty arises either from our clearly recognizing that the truth is absolutely necessary, or that it is necessary only in this world §.113. If we recognize the first with mathematical certainty, then mathematical certainty of the first rank consists therein (certitudo mathematica primi ordinis). In the other case we have mathematical certainty of the second rank (mathematica certitudo secundi ordinis), e.g. in our experiences.
blocks.meier-para-190: The consciousness of the contingency of truth causes uncertainty, and at most only an inexhaustive certainty §.189.113. Arbitrary truths (hypothesis) are those whose truth depends on the arbitrary will of human beings, and their arbitrariness does not hinder complete certainty about them.
blocks.meier-para-191: The proof (probatio) is that which is added to a truth so that it may become certain. The ground of proof (probatio materialiter sumta, ratio probans) is the ground from which the truth can be clearly recognized, and these are the marks of truth §.94. The consequence of the proof (probatio formaliter sumta, consequentia) is the connection of the truth with the ground of proof §.15. Every proof accordingly consists of the ground of proof and the consequence, and it can cause either an exhaustive or an inexhaustive certainty §.159. If the first, it is called a sufficient proof or a demonstration (probatio sufficiens, demonstratio); if the other, it is an insufficient proof (probatio insufficiens). The latter is treated at length in the logic of probable cognition.
blocks.meier-para-192: The cognition of a truth is either a demonstrable (cognitio demonstrabilis) or an indemonstrable cognition (cognitio indemonstrabilis). The latter becomes certain to us as soon as we cognize it distinctly, the former not. The latter is fully certain without proof, the former not. One must take care that one hold neither begged cognition nor demonstrable cognition to be indemonstrable §.168.
blocks.meier-para-193: If we wish to attain exhaustive certainty of a truth by means of proof and from it, or if a proof is to be a demonstration, §.191; then 1) every ground of proof contained in the proof must be exhaustively certain. All demonstrable grounds of proof must accordingly be proved again until one arrives at nothing but indemonstrable grounds of proof; 2) the consequence must be exhaustively certain §.191. Beyond these two items nothing further is required for a proof if it is to be a demonstration §.15.
blocks.meier-para-194: If 1) even a single ground of proof in a proof is false, or 2) uncertain, 3) a single consequence in the proof is false, or 4) uncertain, or 5) if several of these faults are found together in a proof, it cannot be a demonstration §.193.
blocks.meier-para-195: Just as someone can hold an insufficient proof to be a demonstration, so someone can also hold a demonstration to be an insufficient proof, or even a false proof §.165. Consequently one must not reject a demonstration at all merely because it does not have the proper effect on our mind.
blocks.meier-para-196: Through a demonstration we seek to become certain either that something is true, or that something is false §.191. 156. In the first case one can demonstrate a truth in two ways: 1) in an immediate way (demonstratio directa, ostensiva), when we derive the truth from its marks; 2) in a mediate way (demonstratio indirecta, apogogica, deductio ad absurdum), when we demonstrate the incorrectness of its opposite and infer its truth from that. In the same way one can demonstrate that something is false, or refute it (refutatio), a) in a mediate way (refutatio mediata), when we demonstrate the truth of its opposite; b) in an immediate way (refutatio immediata), when we derive its incorrectness from its marks. But one can prove that something is false: α) when we prove that it is impossible and groundless, β) that it is contrary to other undeniable truths, and γ) that something false follows from it.
blocks.meier-para-197: A demonstration causes either a distinctly or an indistinctly exhaustive certainty §.191. 188. The latter are the aesthetic demonstrations (demonstratio aesthetica), the former the logical, philosophical and learned ones (demonstratio logica, philosophica, erudita). A logical demonstration which causes a mathematical certainty is a mathematical demonstration (demonstratio mathematica) §.161.
blocks.meier-para-198: We can always infer: 1) if the whole proof is correct and certain, then the thing proved is also correct and certain; 2) if the thing proved is false and uncertain, then there is a fault in the proof §.194. But we cannot infer: 1) if the proof is false, then the thing proved is also false; 2) if the proof is uncertain, then the thing proved is also only uncertain; 3) what we cannot prove is false; 4) if the thing proved is true and certain, then the proof is also true and certain.
blocks.meier-para-199: The spirit of demonstration (spiritus demonstrationis) consists in a person's sufficient skill in demonstrating, and the natural drive for such a certain cognition as one attains by demonstrating. Without this spirit no one can demonstrate, and no one should venture upon this matter without it.
blocks.meier-para-200: Excessive love of demonstrating is the mania for demonstration (pruritus demonstrandi). This learned sickness shows itself in the following items: 1) when one seeks to demonstrate what one cannot and may not demonstrate; 2) when one even demonstrates in a spurious way, merely to arouse the semblance of demonstrating among the dull-witted; 3) when one stops at mere demonstrating, and does not properly use and apply the demonstrated truths; 4) when one is a pedant in demonstrating, or wholly despises whatever is not demonstrated, whether it is actually not demonstrated, or we merely do not hold it to be so; 5) when one, like a charlatan, exalts demonstrating too highly, and makes too much boasting of it, even when one demonstrates useless trifles.
blocks.meier-para-201: A sensation (sensatio) is a representation of a present thing, and in that we sense something clearly, we experience it. Experience (experientia) therefore consists in that cognition which is clear through sensing. Clear sensations are immediate experience (experientia immediata), and the remaining clear cognition, which is derived from immediate experience by a shorter proof, is called mediate experience (experientia mediata). E.g. that I think is a sensation and immediate experience, but that I have a faculty of thinking is a mediate experience.
blocks.meier-para-202: When something is certain to us, it is certain to us either from experience, or from other grounds, and in the first case either from our own experience, or from the experience of other people. Consequently we have a threefold source of all proofs §.191, namely our own experience, the experience of other people, and other grounds which are not experiences.
blocks.meier-para-203: When we conduct a proof 1) from our own immediate experience, we need only represent clearly a single case in which we have sensed something §.201. 2) In proofs from mediate experience, not only must at least one immediate experience be adduced, but the remaining grounds of proof together with the consequence must also be certain §.201. 193. 3) That of which we are certain even through immediate experience is not an indemonstrable cognition §.192. 201. 4) Experience gives us an exhaustive certainty, in that it contains all the marks of the truth of the object §.201. 94. 96. 5) Experience gives us only an exhaustive certainty of the second rank §.189, and 6) it represents the truth to us only from the external marks §.94.
blocks.meier-para-204: When we prove a truth from other grounds of proof which are not experience, we conduct a proof from reason (probatio ex ratione). In such a proof 1) no ground of proof may occur which is an experience, and 2) all its grounds of proof must be exhaustively certain without experience, if it is to be a demonstration §.193.
blocks.meier-para-205: All experience, and what we prove from it, is cognition from behind (cognitio a posteriore), but the remaining rational cognition is called cognition from before (cognitio a priore). When we are certain of a truth both from our own experience and from reason, this is called the union of reason and experience (connubium rationis et experientiae).
blocks.meier-para-206: From the experience of other people we become certain by means of belief. Whoever gives out an actual thing as true, so that another may also hold it to be true, is called a witness (testis), and his action a testimony (testimonium, testari). To believe (credere) means to accept something on account of a testimony. Belief (fides, fides historica) is the assent which we give to a thing on account of a testimony. The object of belief consists in past, present and future things, but not in other truths.
blocks.meier-para-207: The authority of a witness (autoritas testis) consists in that degree of his honor by means of which he is held worthy of imitation in his cognition. We cannot believe a witness who has no authority with us. And this authority consists 1) in the competence of the witness (dexteritas testis), when he possesses sufficient powers not only to obtain a correct experience, but also to designate it in a correct manner; 2) in the sincerity of the witness (sinceritas testis), or in the inclination of his will to designate his experiences as he holds them to be true. Neither of the two can, without the other, procure for a witness the proper authority.
blocks.meier-para-208: An eyewitness (testis oculatus) is a witness who has himself experienced the thing to which he testifies. A hearsay witness (testis auritus) is no eyewitness, but has only learned of the thing from the testimony of others.
blocks.meier-para-209: For the competence of an eyewitness the following is required: 1) he must have been present at the thing to which he testifies; 2) he must be in a position to obtain a correct experience; 3) he must have a good and faithful memory, or write down his experiences at once; 4) he must possess the gift of designating his own cognition in a correct and sufficient manner.
blocks.meier-para-210: A hearsay witness is, with regard to the testimony which he bears, an eyewitness, and he must accordingly possess all the competence required for that §.209. Insofar as he is a hearsay witness, however, the following items are required for his competence: 1) he must repeat only the testimonies of competent eyewitnesses, and must therefore always be able to name a competent eyewitness who is his authority. A common report (fama) is a testimony of many hearsay witnesses about a thing whose eyewitness is unknown. These hearsay witnesses live either at one time, and then their report is a public rumor (rumor sine capite), or at different times, and then it is an oral tradition (oralis traditio). The common report lacks the necessary authority; 2) he must possess understanding enough to grasp rightly what he hears or reads; 3) he must possess a faithful memory, in order to communicate the information to others just as he received it.
blocks.meier-para-211: In the sincerity of a witness it depends merely on his good will not to lie §.207. That witness who promises himself from a true testimony either nothing but good, or more good than evil, and who promises himself from lying nothing but evil, or more evil than good, speaks the truth. And in the opposite case he lies. This good or evil can concern his soul or his body, or his external condition; he may hope or fear it from GOD, from those people to whom he gives the testimony, or of whom he testifies, etc., whether he deceives himself in this matter or not.
blocks.meier-para-212: The certainty of a testimony rests 1) on the internal marks of its truth §.95. 96; 2) on the external marks of its truth, namely on the sufficient authority of the witness, which must at least be very probable §.207, 94. The testimonies of a competent and sincere witness cannot be false.
blocks.meier-para-213: What we believe, we do not beg §.212. 168. Unbelief (incredulitas) is the habit of not believing a certain or probable testimony. Credulity (credulitas) is the habit of believing an improbable testimony. Both faults are unreasonable §.174.
blocks.meier-para-214: A witness is credible (testis fide dignus) if one can recognize in a learned manner, at least probably, that he has sufficient authority; the testimony of such a witness is a credible testimony (testimonium fide dignum). Reasonable or seeing belief (fides oculata, rationalis) is the habit of believing only credible witnesses.
blocks.meier-para-215: There is 1) a union of experience and belief (connubium experientiae et fidei), when we cognize something both from our own experience and from credible testimonies; 2) a union of belief and reason (connubium fidei et rationis), when we are certain of a thing both from reason and through belief; and 3) a union of reason, belief and experience (connubium rationis experientiae et fidei), when we cognize a truth convincingly by all three ways. The union of belief with the remaining sources of cognition is also called mixed belief (fides mixta); but when we accept something solely for the sake of belief, it is called pure belief (fides pura). Because we can demonstrate neither the competence nor the sincerity of human witnesses, belief gives only a probability, and at most only a moral certainty §.175. Of practical learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-216: A cognition is practical (cognitio practica) insofar as it can move us in a noticeable way to do or to omit an action. All more perfect cognition which is not practical is called a speculative cognition (cognitio speculativa, speculatio). All learned cognition is accordingly either practical or speculative.
blocks.meier-para-217: A cognition in which we represent to ourselves that something should be done or omitted is also called practical, insofar as it is opposed to theoretical cognition (cognitio theoretica, theoria), the cognition which does not represent to us that something should be done or omitted. All learned cognition is either practical or theoretical, and both kinds belong either to practical or to speculative cognition §.216.
blocks.meier-para-218: Practical cognition is better than speculative cognition §.216, because in it a greater agreement of the manifold is found §.22. Whoever, then, wants to improve his learned cognition as far as possible must avoid speculation, and seek nothing but practical cognition.
blocks.meier-para-219: No true learned cognition is speculative by its nature, but only on account of the lack of insight of a scholar, who cannot see, or will not see, its connection with human conduct. In the latter case the scholar disgraces himself.
blocks.meier-para-220: It is unreasonable to want to hold as speculation: 1) all profound, determinate, precise and difficult learned cognition; 2) all learning in general; 3) all theory; 4) that learned cognition which is not practical in this or that person; 5) all cognition which does not have an immediate influence on the moral conduct of a person.
blocks.meier-para-221: A cognition is practical either on account of its object (cognitio obiective practica), or on account of its constitution (cognitio subiective practica), or both at once. In the first case it must have an object which can be cognized as is required for a practical cognition. In the other case it is so constituted that it can act upon the faculty of desire.
blocks.meier-para-222: A learned cognition is practical on account of its object: 1) when the truths cognized are good and useful. And in this respect all true learned cognition is practical §.39. 221.
blocks.meier-para-223: A learned cognition is practical on account of its object: 2) insofar as it underlies the rational actions by which human perfection is preserved §.221, and whose lack one notices at once in a person's actions.
blocks.meier-para-224: A learned cognition is practical on account of its object: 3) when its object consists in the rules which we must observe if we want to preserve our entire welfare in the best manner §.221.
blocks.meier-para-225: A learned cognition is practical on account of its object: 4) when its object has, in a remote and mediate way, an influence on our entire good conduct §.221, e.g. the cognition of such truths without which the remaining practical truths §.222-224 could not be cognized by us human beings either at all, or at least not in a learned manner.
blocks.meier-para-226: Because no human being is in a position to cognize all practical truths, that learned cognition is called preeminently and absolutely practical (cognitio obiective et comparative s. eminenter practica) which is practical in a higher degree, e.g. which is noticeably more useful to us than another, and which has an immediate or very near influence on our conduct.
blocks.meier-para-227: All learned cognition is called comparatively speculative (cognitio comparative speculativa) if it is practical in a very small degree. E.g. 1) if it has a very small and imperceptible influence on our regular conduct; 2) if it has a very small utility; 3) if it hinders us from a more necessary and more useful cognition.
blocks.meier-para-228: On account of the differing way of life and principal science, a learned cognition can rightly be held by one person to be practical, and by another to be speculative §.226. 227. Indeed, someone may, on account of his meager powers of cognition, and from negligence, fail to see the connection of a learned cognition with our conduct, and will therefore hold it to be a speculative cognition.
blocks.meier-para-229: Insofar as a learned cognition is practical, so far is it also useful. One must accordingly 1) hold no truth and no learned cognition to be wholly useless §.222. 2) A learned cognition is not useless merely because it is of no use to this or that person, and is perhaps even harmful to him. 3) A learned cognition which is not useful in one respect can be useful in another respect. 4) One must not infer: what is not useful to us now will also not be useful to us in the future.
blocks.meier-para-230: The more utilities a learned cognition procures, the greater they are, and the greater and more manifold its influence on our entire conduct, the more practical it is §.216.
blocks.meier-para-231: In order that every scholar may improve his learned cognition as far as possible, he must 1) cognize most perfectly those truths which are practical in the highest degree. The degree of diligence and of perfection of learned cognition must be proportioned to the degree of the practical in its object §.70. 2) Each must, where possible, choose for his principal science that part of learning which is practical in the highest degree §.63.
blocks.meier-para-232: A cognition which is practical according to its constitution is called a living and moving cognition (cognitio viva, movens). A living rational cognition (cognitio rationalis viva) is a rational cognition which is so constituted that rational desires and aversions are awakened through it; or it contains motives (motiva), that is, such rational representations of the good and evil through which desires and aversions arise. All rational cognition which is not so constituted is called a dead rational cognition (cognitio rationalis mortua).
blocks.meier-para-233: That constitution of cognition by virtue of which it effects desires and aversions is called the life of cognition (cognitionis vita), which, when it consists in the motives §.232, is called the rational life of cognition, or then the cognition moves and stirs in a rational manner (vita rationalis cognitionis).
blocks.meier-para-234: A learned cognition can 1) with regard to its object be uncommonly practical, and nevertheless dead; 2) it can be false and uncommonly living; the life of cognition is therefore no mark of its truth; 3) a learned cognition can be very extensive, great, correct, certain and distinct, and nevertheless dead §.232. Life is accordingly yet another perfection of learned cognition, which is different from all its remaining perfections.
blocks.meier-para-235: The practical in learned cognition becomes actually practical only through life. Living rational cognition is accordingly more perfect than dead, even if both should otherwise be adorned with all the remaining logical perfections in equal degree.
blocks.meier-para-236: If rational and learned cognition is to move rationally, it must 1) be an intuitive cognition. A cognition is intuitive (cognitio intuitiva) when we represent the object more strongly than its signs; but if we represent these more strongly than the former, the cognition is symbolic (cognitio symbolica). All learned cognition is either intuitive or symbolic. When one occupies attention, reflection and deliberation chiefly with the object of learned cognition, it becomes a distinct intuitive cognition.
blocks.meier-para-237: Pleasure (voluptas) is the intuitive cognition of perfection, and the intuitive cognition of imperfection is displeasure (taedium). A cognition causes us indifference (indifferentia) when it causes us neither pleasure nor displeasure. If, then, rational and learned cognition is to move rationally, it must 2) awaken pleasure and displeasure; a) about itself it must awaken in us nothing but pleasure: because by virtue of all the rules of logic it must be uncommonly perfect, and the feeling of its perfection must drive us to desire and to attain it. Whoever, then, is indifferent whether he cognizes a thing in a learned way or not, his learned cognition is not living.
blocks.meier-para-238: Rational and learned cognition, if it is to move rationally, must b) awaken about the object either pleasure, or vexation, or both at once, in that it represents the object to us in an intuitive manner either as good, or as evil, or as both at once. Then the learned cognition contains motives §.232; not only to desire itself §.237, but also either to desire or to abhor its object.
blocks.meier-para-239: If rational and learned cognition is to move us rationally, it must 3) represent to us in a learned manner that all the good and all the evil on account of which it pleases or displeases us will actually be in our subsequent states.
blocks.meier-para-240: If rational and learned cognition is to move us rationally, it must 4) represent to us in a learned manner that it is within our power, or can be within our power, to make actual the good on account of which it pleases us, and to prevent the evil on account of which it causes us displeasure.
blocks.meier-para-241: If learned cognition is to be properly living, it must 1) cause no equilibrium, or at least soon remove it. We stand, namely, in an equilibrium (aequilibrium) when the motives on both sides are equal and opposed to one another; 2) it must outweigh the sensible life of indistinct cognition, or the latter must not contradict it at all.
blocks.meier-para-242: If rational and learned cognition is properly living, it causes a powerful and lasting resolution, which breaks out in deed, in that we actually act as accords with the learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-243: The genuine life of learned cognition (vita vera cognitionis eruditae) consists in its true use (usus verus cognitionis eruditae), when we effect all its true utilities, or make ourselves in fact more perfect through it. But if we make ourselves thereby more imperfect or only apparently more perfect, its misuse (abusus cognitionis eruditae) consists therein, and that is its spurious life (vita cognitionis eruditae spuria). A perfect learned cognition must be living in a genuine way.
blocks.meier-para-244: The more and greater motives a learned cognition contains, the better they are cognized, and the more and greater desires and aversions are awakened through it, the more living is the learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-245: One must not infer: 1) the learned cognition which does not move me does not move others either; 2) that which moves me moves others also.
blocks.meier-para-246: The lack of life of learned cognition arises from ignorance §.236-240. 41. According as the latter is either necessary or contingent, praiseworthy or blameworthy §.43.50. 51, so also is the lack of life constituted. It cannot be demanded that all learned cognition move constantly and in equal degree.
blocks.meier-para-247: The greater and more practical the objects are, the more strongly their learned cognition must move; the smaller and less practical they are, the less their learned cognition must move §.70. All our learned cognition must move us in some respect §.237.
blocks.meier-para-248: Each person must choose for his principal science that part of learning which by its nature is capable of the most living learned cognition; and each must seek to cognize his principal science most livingly §.63. 64. Of learned concepts.
blocks.meier-para-249: A concept (conceptus) is a representation of a thing in a being which possesses the faculty of thinking. All our representations are accordingly concepts.
blocks.meier-para-250: As many different kinds of cognition as there are, so many different kinds of concepts there are also §.249. Consequently concepts are either learned concepts (conceptus eruditus, logicus), or not §.21. The former is a distinct concept that is logically perfect to a noticeable degree. An unlearned concept (conceptus ineruditus) is a concept that possesses no noticeable degree of logical perfection. And then it is either a beautiful concept, or not §.19. The former is an aesthetic concept (conceptus pulcher, aestheticus), the latter however a common one (conceptus vulgaris). A learned concept is either at the same time beautiful, or not. The latter is a merely learned concept (conceptus mere eruditus). The former, however, is a concept that is not merely learned (conceptus non mere eruditus). And concepts of this kind are the best concepts §.32.
blocks.meier-para-251: A learned concept must conform as far as possible to the rules of extensiveness, of magnitude, of truth, of clarity, of certainty, and of the practical character of learned cognition §.41-248.
blocks.meier-para-252: The object of learned concepts is not determined by their nature. Of any possible thing whatever a learned concept is possible §.250.
blocks.meier-para-253: Everyone must improve according to the doctrine of reason chiefly those concepts that belong to his principal science, §.64, and in any system whatever chiefly the principal concepts. It is neither possible nor necessary to improve all our concepts according to the doctrine of reason, and just as little to improve all our learned concepts to an equal degree. The greater a concept is, the more one must improve it §.70.
blocks.meier-para-254: We have only three ways of arriving at concepts: experience, abstraction, and arbitrary combination.
blocks.meier-para-255: All our sensations are concepts §.249. 201. A concept of experience (conceptus per experientiam formatus) is a concept that we obtain through experience. E.g. the concepts of the alterations of our soul, of our body, and of other things outside us. We obtain a concept of experience either through immediate or through mediate experience. §.201.
blocks.meier-para-256: Through immediate experience we can obtain only concepts of actual things, insofar as they are present to us, and indeed these concepts contain only affirmative and changeable marks. The mediate concepts of experience can also represent to us other objects, and other things about them. §.201.
blocks.meier-para-257: Because concepts of experience can be learned only insofar as they are distinct §.250, one must analyze them carefully §.142. And this work is often furthered 1) by the use of the weapons of the senses, e.g. magnifying glasses. 2) By the anatomy of corporeal things, whereby one cognizes the parts and the manner of their composition. And thereby one obtains the concept of the essence of a corporeal thing. 3) By attention to that from which a thing arises and how it arises, when one is present at its arising, and from this one also obtains concepts of the essence. 4) When one seeks to experience the object often in different circumstances: for then one discovers the best marks more easily, whereby the concept of experience becomes complete.
blocks.meier-para-258: All concepts of experience are true and certain §.202, and they represent to us the objects as they are constituted, because otherwise we would be inhabitants of another world. But if we hold a concept to be a concept of experience that is not one, or something to be an object of the concept of experience that is not one: then it does indeed seem as if the concept of experience were false, but the error lies in another concept.
blocks.meier-para-259: We make a concept through logical abstraction (conceptus per abstractionem logicam formatus) when we hold up against one another concordant concepts of different things, and represent distinctly to ourselves alone the marks that they have in common with one another. To this end 1) let one take some concepts that are different and at the same time similar. E.g. a rational animal and an irrational animal; 2) let one analyze each of them §.142; 3) let one abstract the marks that are different in them, or obscure them; 4) let one gather the remaining marks together into one concept, e.g. an animal.
blocks.meier-para-260: All concepts that are made through logical abstraction are abstracted or abstract concepts (conceptus abstractus, notio). Concepts that are not abstracted are called singular concepts (conceptus singularis, idea). E.g. Leibniz. All immediate concepts of experience are singular concepts §.255.201. What is represented as a mark of another is contained in it and belongs to it (in altero contineri, ipsi convenire). The abstracted concept is therefore contained in all those concepts from which it can be abstracted §.259. The abstracted concept contains under itself those from which it was abstracted, and these are contained under it (conceptus alios sub se continet, et conceptus sub alio continentur seu ad eum referuntur).
blocks.meier-para-261: An abstracted concept is called a higher concept (conceptus superior) insofar as it contains others under itself; but insofar as a concept is contained under another, it is called a lower concept (conceptus inferior). The lower concept always contains marks that are not contained in the higher §.259, and these are called the difference of the lower concepts (differentia conceptus inferioris). An abstracted concept that comprehends under itself only singular concepts is called a species (species), but one that also contains abstracted concepts under itself is called a genus (genus).
blocks.meier-para-262: The aggregate of all concepts that are contained under an abstracted concept is its extension (sphaera notionis). The more abstract and higher a concept is, that is: the more often logical abstraction has been repeated in its case, the greater is its extension. An abstracted concept belongs either to more concepts than those that are contained under another, or to fewer, or to neither. In the first case it is a wider concept than the other (conceptus latior), in the second a narrower (conceptus angustior), and in the third they are reciprocal concepts (conceptus reciproci), of which neither is wider than the other. Insofar as an abstracted concept belongs to all that are contained under another, it is called a universal concept (conceptus universalis), but insofar as it does not belong to all of them, a particular one (conceptus particularis). An abstracted concept can be called a higher and lower, wider and narrower, universal and particular concept in different respects. Every abstracted concept is universal in a certain respect. Abstract learned cognition is therefore called universal learned cognition (cognitio erudita universalis).
blocks.meier-para-263: In universal cognition one can 1) infer: What belongs to or contradicts the higher concepts, that also belongs to or contradicts all lower concepts that are contained under them. §.260. 2) One cannot infer: what belongs to or contradicts a lower concept, that also belongs to or contradicts other lower concepts that belong with it to a higher concept. §.261. 3) One can infer: what belongs to or contradicts all and each of the lower concepts, that also belongs to or contradicts their higher concept §.259. 261.
blocks.meier-para-264: Abstract cognition furthers 1) the distinctness and completeness of cognition §.143. For the more abstract it is, the less it contains in itself §.259, and the more easily it can therefore be thought through without much confusion; 2) the extensiveness of cognition §.263. 25. 3) The thoroughness of cognition §.263. 163. 4) The utility and use of learned cognition §.39.
blocks.meier-para-265: An abstracted concept contains nothing that is not contained in the lower concepts §.259; if these are true, then, it cannot possibly be false. If one wishes, then, to prove an abstracted concept, one need only show that it was abstracted from true concepts. If one abstracts from a false concept the marks that contradict the rest, one obtains a true concept §.95.
blocks.meier-para-266: A concept is made through learned arbitrary combination (combinatio conceptuum arbitraria, logica, erudita, philosophica, rationalis) when one represents to oneself as One two concepts of which one has cognized in a learned way that they are not repugnant to one another. To this end let one take 1) an abstracted concept, whether one has already abstracted it long ago, or only now abstracts it; 2) a difference of a lower concept, of which we are either already convinced, or are convinced only afterwards, that it does not contradict the abstracted concept. This difference has either been left out through the abstraction from the abstract concept, or not. In the first case we obtain a lower concept from which we have abstracted the abstract one; in the second, however, a new lower concept; 3) let one represent to oneself the abstract concept, taken together with this difference, as One concept.
blocks.meier-para-267: A learned concept that has been made through arbitrary combination must be proved or refuted. Both happen 1) from experience, when one shows that its objects either are actual or are not actual; 2) from reason, either in a mediate or immediate way §.196. E.g. when one shows either that, and how, its objects can become actual, or that they cannot become actual.
blocks.meier-para-268: A definition, or a logical definition (definitio, definitio logica), is a determinate concept of a thing. The object of the definition is the defined thing, or the defined concept (definitum) §.151.
blocks.meier-para-269: A description (descriptio) is an indeterminate concept, and it is either a complete or a complete description §.151 (descriptio completa, vel incompleta). No description is a definition, and still less must it be held to be one §.268. Meanwhile they can be very perfect, useful and necessary learned concepts.
blocks.meier-para-270: Definitions must conform to six rules: 1) A definition must conform to the rules of the extensiveness of learned cognition. §.41-65. Consequently it must be a complete concept. §.268.151. 55. Consequently a) it must contain in itself no fewer marks than are required for a complete concept; nor b) more than are necessary.§.269. Hence the definition, among all possible complete concepts of a thing, must be the very shortest, that is: contain as few marks as completeness permits. c) It must not be wider than the defined thing §.262, consequently its marks taken together must belong to no other thing than the defined thing alone. d) It must not be narrower than the defined thing. §.262. Consequently the defined concept and the definition are reciprocal concepts §.262.
blocks.meier-para-271: If in a system one defines the higher concepts before the lower, then, when one is to define a concept that is not the highest, one can compose its definition from the nearest higher concept and from the difference §.261. Thereby the definitions become short and complete, the definitions hang together more systematically, they are more conformable to the nature of the lower concepts, and they pave an easier way to the demonstrations.
blocks.meier-para-272: Because the defined concept and the definition are reciprocal concepts §.270, one can infer: 1) To whom the defined concept belongs, to him the definition also belongs; 2) to whom the definition belongs, to him the defined concept also belongs; 3) to whom the defined concept does not belong, to him the definition also does not belong; 4) to whom the definition does not belong, to him the defined concept also does not belong §.262.
blocks.meier-para-273: 2) A definition must conform to the rules of the magnitude of learned cognition. §.66-91. It must therefore consist of the greatest, most important and most fruitful marks, of the essence, essential parts and properties, and, as often as possible, of affirmative marks. §.115-121. It is therefore a fault a) if a definition consists of contingent attributes: then it would not even be a complete concept. §.121. b) If it consists of relations: then it also would be no complete concept. §.121. c) If it consists without necessity of negative marks. If in a system one is to define opposed concepts, then the opposition must be evident from the definitions, and so one of the two must be defined negatively.
blocks.meier-para-274: 3) A definition must conform to the rules of the truth of learned cognition. §.92-114. The truth of definitions moreover requires that they conform to all the rules that must be observed in definitions. A regular definition (definitio legitima) conforms to all the rules of definitions; one that is contrary to one or more of these rules is an irregular definition (definitio illegitima).
blocks.meier-para-275: 4) A definition must conform to all the rules of the distinctness of learned cognition. §.115-155. Yet it can be an incomplete concept. §.147. Since all its marks must be clear §.137, one can presuppose them as clear either partly from common life, partly from other systems; or one must first define them before one puts them as marks into the definition §.268.
blocks.meier-para-276: If a definition is absolutely obscure, or has absolutely obscure marks, then it is no definition at all §.275. 125. But if it is obscure only relatively, or contains marks that are obscure only relatively, then it can indeed be a good definition, but not for him to whom it is obscure §.125.
blocks.meier-para-277: The defined concept is not clearer than it is itself. So that the definition may not become obscure and indistinct §.275, one must take care that the defined concept be set neither as an immediate nor as a mediate mark into its own definition §.116. When the latter happens, this fault is called the circle in defining (circulus in definiendo).
blocks.meier-para-278: 5) A definition must conform to the rules of the certainty of learned cognition §.155-215. Consequently one must prove of any definition whatever a) that it is either a correct concept of experience §.258, or a correct abstracted concept §.265, or a correct arbitrary concept §.267, b) that it is regular §.274.
blocks.meier-para-279: 6) A definition must conform to the rules of practical learned cognition §.216-248. Consequently one must choose for a definition the most important and most fruitful marks, from which can most easily be proved the most useful and serviceable things that we must investigate about the defined thing in order to cognize it in a practical way.
blocks.meier-para-280: A definition either represents the essence of the defined thing, or not §.273. The former is a real definition (definitio realis, genetica), the latter however a nominal definition (definitio nominalis). A nominal definition contains either the essential parts of the defined thing, or its properties §.273. The former is an essential nominal definition (definitio essentialis), the latter however an accidental nominal definition (definitio accidentalis).
blocks.meier-para-281: If one wishes to make a real definition, then 1) let one seek to cognize the essence of the defined thing, either through mediate experience, e.g. §.257, or through abstraction, or through a proof from reason, or through arbitrary combination; 2) let one make of the essence a determinate concept §.280.
blocks.meier-para-282: If one wishes to make a nominal definition, then let one seek 1) to cognize the essential parts or properties of the thing to be defined, either from mediate experience §.256, or through a proof from reason, or from the essence, if it is already known to us. 2) Let one select those essential parts and properties, and as many of them, as are necessary for a perfect regular definition §.270-279.
blocks.meier-para-283: Because the things to be defined can have many essential parts and properties, one can select at pleasure those that make up a nominal definition §.282; if only one otherwise observes the rules of definitions. And insofar nominal definitions are arbitrary.
blocks.meier-para-284: Just as we cannot define all concepts §.139.150. 268, so we also need not define all concepts, but only those that belong within the horizon of our learned cognition, and without whose definition our learned cognition could not attain the required degree of its perfection. The excess in defining is called the mania for defining (pruritus definiendi).
blocks.meier-para-285: The logical division of concepts (divisio logica) consists in a distinct representation of all lower concepts that are opposed to one another and that are contained under one and the same higher concept. This higher concept is called the divided concept (divisum), and the lower concepts the members of the division (membra dividentia). If one wishes accordingly to make a logical division, 1) let one take an abstracted concept; 2) let one find all differences of its lower concepts that are opposed to one another; 3) let one combine these differences, one after another, by an opposition, with the higher concept. E.g. all concepts are either obscure or clear concepts.
blocks.meier-para-286: A division of a member of the division is called a subdivision (subdivisio), and different divisions of a concept, which are made in different respects, are called codivisions (codivisiones). It is clear of itself what the divided concept of the subdivision (subdivisum), and of the codivisions (codivisum) is. Likewise what the members of the subdivision (membra subdividentia), and of the codivisions (membra codividentia) are.
blocks.meier-para-287: If a logical division is to be correct, then 1) the divided concept must not be wider than the members of the division, when they are taken together by an opposition (disiunctive); or no member of the division must be left out, because otherwise not all lower concepts that are opposed to one another would have been adduced §.285. 262. 2) The divided concept must not be narrower than the members of the division, when they are taken together by an opposition §.262. Otherwise one would mix among the members of the division a concept that is no lower concept of the divided concept §.285. Consequently the divided concept and the members of the division, when they are taken together by an opposition, are reciprocal concepts §.262, and the division must exhaust the divided concept.
blocks.meier-para-288: 3) The members of the division must be so opposed that none belongs to another §.285. 260. 4) The divided concept must not contradict any member of the division: for it is contained in it §.285. 260. 5) The members of the subdivision must not be placed among the members of the division: otherwise not all members would be opposed to one another n. 3. 4. §.286. 6) The number of the members of the division must be determined solely by the nature of the divided concept, and the aim in which it is divided.
blocks.meier-para-289: To whom the divided concept belongs, to him One member of the division also belongs; to whom One member of the division belongs, to him the divided concept also belongs; to whom the divided concept does not belong, to him none of the members of the division belongs; to whom none of the members of the division belongs, to him the divided concept also does not belong §.287.
blocks.meier-para-290: Logical divisions 1) further the invention of learned concepts through arbitrary combination §.285. 266. 2) Serve us to put our abstracted concepts into a proper order and connection, and to retain them the more easily; 3) convince us of the universality of our abstract cognition.
blocks.meier-para-291: One must take care in divisions not to heap them up too much, together with their subdivisions, because otherwise a great confusion arises; and one must avoid in them everything forced. On learned judgments.
blocks.meier-para-292: Concepts that belong to one another §.260 agree with one another; but those that do not belong to one another are repugnant to one another, or conflict with one another (repugnare). The agreement and the conflict of several concepts are the logical relations of concepts (logica conceptuum relatio). A judgment (iudicium) is a representation of a logical relation of some concepts; and insofar as everything is abstracted from it without which its truth can be cognized in a learned way, it is called a logical judgment (iudicium logicum), which is a learned judgment (iudicium eruditum) if it conforms, as far as possible, to all the rules of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-293: That concept of which we represent to ourselves in a judgment that another belongs or does not belong to it, is the subject (subiectum); the other, on the contrary, of which we represent to ourselves that it belongs or does not belong to the subject, is the predicate (praedicatum). The representation of the agreement of several concepts is the concept of connection (copula). Negation (negatio) is the representation of the absence of a thing, and the representation of the absence of the concept of connection is the negation of the concept of connection (negatio copulae). It is therefore the representation of the conflict of the predicate with the subject §.292.
blocks.meier-para-294: In a logical judgment we represent to ourselves either that the predicate belongs to the subject, or does not belong §.292. 293. The former is an affirmative judgment (iudicium affirmans, affirmativum), the latter a negative one (iudicium negans, negativum). E.g. the soul can think, matter cannot think. In a negative judgment there is the negation of the concept of connection §.293. And if in a judgment there is a negation either in the subject or the predicate, or in both at once, provided only that the concept of connection is not negated, it is an affirmative judgment, which is called an infinite judgment (iudicium infinitum). One can therefore transform all negative judgments into affirmative ones, if one moves the negation away from the concept of connection to the predicate. E.g. the soul is not mortal, the soul is immortal. The quality of judgments (qualitas iudicii) consists in their affirmation and negation.
blocks.meier-para-295: An affirmative judgment is true if the predicate belongs to the subject, and indeed just as the former is affirmed of the latter; but it is false if the predicate does not belong to the subject, or at least does not belong to it in the way in which it is affirmed of it. A negative judgment is true if the predicate does not belong to the subject, and indeed as it is denied of it; but it is false if the predicate belongs to the subject, or at least is not so repugnant to it as it is denied of it §.294. 99. If a true judgment is held to be false, and a false one to be true, it is an erroneous judgment §.109.
blocks.meier-para-296: The truth and incorrectness of a judgment lies in the concept of connection and in the negation of it §.295. 293. Consequently 1) the subject and predicate of a false judgment can be true; 2) the subject and predicate of a true affirmative judgment can be false; 3) the subject can be true and the predicate false, or conversely, in a true negative judgment.
blocks.meier-para-297: All true judgments have a ground, and a sufficient ground, of their truth §.16. This ground is called the condition of judgments (hypothesis, conditio iudicii). Consequently the truth and incorrectness of judgments can be cognized from it. It is therefore the criterion and the proof of truth §.94. 191.
blocks.meier-para-298: The conditions of judgments are 1) either sufficient or insufficient conditions §.297.119. 191; 2) either internal or external conditions §.297. 94; 3) either absolutely necessary or contingent conditions. The former are the essence, the essential parts, the properties or the definition of the subject, and the latter its contingent attributes and relations §.297. 121. 273. If the contingent condition of a judgment is combined with its subject, it is called the determination or limitation of the judgment (determinatio et limitatio iudicii).
blocks.meier-para-299: If the condition of a judgment 1) is an internal, absolutely necessary and sufficient condition, then it is inseparable from the subject. Whether one thinks it or not, it is there nonetheless, and consequently the predicate also belongs or does not belong to the subject, according as it is either affirmed or denied. Truth then does not require that one combine this condition with the judgment §.295. But if it is 2) a contingent condition, then it is now there, now not there, and the judgment would be now true, now not true. Truth therefore requires that one combine these conditions with the judgment. A determinate judgment (iudicium determinatum, limitatum) is a judgment that has a determination; a judgment that is not determinate is an indeterminate judgment (iudicium indeterminatum, illimitatum).
blocks.meier-para-300: The analysis of a judgment (analysis, resolutio iudicii) consists in this, that one gives heed one after another to all parts of it. All judgments can be analyzed §.139, and through this work one finds not only the proofs of judgments §.297; but one also learns to grasp them properly, and to present them to others.
blocks.meier-para-301: The subject of a judgment is either a singular or an abstract concept §.293. 260. The former is a singular judgment (iudicium singulare), the latter a common judgment (iudicium commune). In which the predicate is affirmed or denied either of all those contained under the subject, or of some. The former is a universal judgment (iudicium universale), the latter a particular judgment (iudicium particulare). The latter is either at the same time universally true, a not merely particular judgment (iudicium non tantum particulare), or not, a merely particular judgment (iudicium tantum particulare). All these judgments either affirm or deny §.294. The universal affirmative judgments are called A; the universal negative E; the particular affirmative I; and the particular negative O. The predicate of all universal judgments is, in respect of the subject, a universal concept, because negative ones can be transformed into affirmative ones §.294. 262. And because in singular as well as in universal judgments it is judged that the predicate belongs to the whole subject or not, one can count the singular judgments among the universal ones. Insofar as a judgment is either a singular or a common one, insofar one ascribes to it a magnitude (quantitas iudicii).
blocks.meier-para-302: A universal affirmative judgment is true if the predicate belongs to all those contained under the subject §.301. 295. It is therefore false if the predicate belongs to not a single one of those contained under the subject, or does not belong to some, or even to only a single one of them. A universal negative judgment is true if the predicate is repugnant to all those contained under the subject §.301. 295. It is therefore false if the predicate belongs to all those contained under the subject, or to some of them, or even to only a single one of them.
blocks.meier-para-303: If the sufficient condition of a common judgment 1) is absolutely necessary in the subject, then it is inseparable from it, and is found wherever the subject is found, consequently in all those contained under it §.263. Then the judgment is therefore universally true, for where the condition is, there the predicate is also §.299. If, therefore, a predicate is affirmed or denied of an abstract concept on account of its essence, or essential part, or property, or definition, then the judgment is universally true §.298. 299. 2) If this condition is a determination, then it becomes absolutely necessary as soon as it is combined with the subject, because thereby all things to which this determination does not belong are excluded from it §.299. And thus the determinate judgment is universally true.
blocks.meier-para-304: A judgment has either only One subject and One predicate, or several. The former is a simple judgment (iudicium simplex), the latter however a composite one (iudicium compositum). If the subject and predicate are composed of several concepts, then either some of them are thought for the sake of the rest, or none is thought for the sake of another. In the first case the concepts for whose sake the rest are thought are the principal subjects and principal predicates (subiectum et praedicatum principale), and the rest the secondary subjects and secondary predicates (subiectum et praedicatum minus principale). In the other case the composite judgment is a copulative judgment (iudicium copulativum).
blocks.meier-para-305: A judgment that affirms that a judgment follows from the condition, without that or this being declared true or false, is a conditional judgment (iudicium hypotheticum, conditionale). The condition of conditional judgments is called the first, or preceding (prius, antecedens), but the judgment that follows from it the last or following (posterius, consequens). Not all judgments that have a condition are therefore conditional §.297.
blocks.meier-para-306: For the truth of conditional judgments it is not required that the first and the last be true; but that it have a correct consequence, or that the first be the sufficient ground of the truth of the last. In the opposite case the conditional judgment is false §.305. 295.
blocks.meier-para-307: A disjunctive judgment (iudicium disiunctivum) is a judgment that affirms that among several judgments one is true and the rest are false, but in such a way that it is not determined which is true and which false. The several judgments of which it is composed are called the members of the disjunction, or of the opposition (membra disiunctionis, disiunctiva), e.g. the soul is either simple, or composite.
blocks.meier-para-308: If a disjunctive judgment is to be true, then the members of the disjunction must relate to one another just as one represents to oneself in it §.295. Consequently 1) not more than one member must be true. If therefore all members or even only two are true at the same time, then the judgment is false; 2) One member must necessarily be true; if therefore all members are false, or one is true only contingently, then the judgment is false; 3) no member must be left out, for if the omitted one were also false, it would nevertheless not be evident from the disjunction that among those adduced One is necessarily true §.307.
blocks.meier-para-309: The representation of the manner and way in which the predicate belongs or does not belong to the subject is the determination of the concept of connection and of the negation of it (modus formalis). A judgment has either such a determination, or not. The former is an impure judgment (iudicium modale, modificatum, complexum qua copulam), the latter however a pure judgment (iudicium purum), e.g. this world exists necessarily, it does not exist necessarily. In the truth of impure judgments one must pay particular attention to the determination of the concept of connection and of the negation of it.
blocks.meier-para-310: A judgment that is composed of an affirmative and a negative one in a very hidden way is called an exponible judgment (iudicium exponibile). If it is to be true, then both judgments must be correct, and one must accordingly analyze it in order to make sure of this. E.g. GOD alone is absolutely immortal.
blocks.meier-para-311: The judgments that at the same time represent the state of the mind with respect to a certain judgment are judgments that are not logical (iudicia non logica). For example: O how greatly the sinner deceives himself! Such judgments are very practical, and so that learned cognition may not become merely learned, one must take care that not all learned judgments be simple or merely logical.
blocks.meier-para-312: All learned judgments are either judgments of consideration (iudicia theoretica), or judgments of practice (iudicia practica) §.217. The latter judge that something should be done or left undone, e.g. we must observe the laws; the former however do not, e.g. virtue makes us happy.
blocks.meier-para-313: All learned judgments are either demonstrable (iudicia demonstrativa), or indemonstrable judgments (iudicia indemonstrabilia). The truth of the latter is evident from themselves as soon as we cognize them distinctly; the former, however, cannot be certain without proof §.192.
blocks.meier-para-314: The predicate of an affirmative judgment is either identical with the subject, or it is different from it. The former is an empty judgment (iudicium identicum), which is either wholly empty (iudicium ex toto identicum), or in part (iudicium ex parte identicum). The predicate of the former is not at all different from the subject, but the predicate of the latter is only a part of the subject. Because no concept is repugnant to itself, we cognize the truth of all empty judgments as soon as we understand them §.295; they are therefore indemonstrable §.313. If a judgment is not empty, one must fear that between the subject and predicate there could be so great a difference that they do not belong to one another. Consequently they are not indemonstrable, and there are therefore, besides the empty ones, no indemonstrable judgments §.313.
blocks.meier-para-315: Indemonstrable judgments are either judgments of consideration, or judgments of practice. The former are fundamental judgments (axioma), the latter however postulated judgments (postulatum). One must hold no demonstrable judgment to be an indemonstrable one §.313.
blocks.meier-para-316: As often as we affirm a concept of itself, or a part of it of it, so often we have a fundamental judgment §.315.314. One can therefore find fundamental judgments from definitions, if one affirms of the defined concept: 1) the whole definition, and insofar logical definitions are indemonstrable; 2) some marks of the definition; 3) the individual marks of it §.268.
blocks.meier-para-317: As often as I represent to myself a thing that one can regard as an effect, and I affirm of him who wishes to produce it that he must produce it or a part of it, so I have a postulated judgment §.315.314. If therefore the defined concept can be regarded as an effect, and I affirm of him who wishes to produce it that he must produce 1) the whole definition, 2) or some marks, or 3) individual marks: so I find postulated judgments from the definitions §.268.
blocks.meier-para-318: In a demonstration from reason all proofs must be completely certain §.193.204; they are therefore either demonstrable or not §.313. In the first case they must be proved again. Consequently a proof does not become a demonstration until I arrive at nothing but indemonstrable proofs. Empty judgments, fundamental judgments and postulated judgments are therefore the first beginnings of all demonstrations from reason §.314. 315. Then the understanding comes completely to rest, when the proof has been carried back to such judgments.
blocks.meier-para-319: Demonstrable judgments are either certain merely through experience, or not. The former are intuitive judgments (iudicium intuitivum), the latter however derivative judgments (iudicium discursivum). The intuitive judgment consists of nothing but concepts of experience, and is an immediate experience §.201, and a singular judgment §.301. No intuitive judgment is indemonstrable §.313. 314, for I must always recall a single case, and thereby cognize how and whether I have arrived at such a judgment without deception §.202. All intuitive judgments are the first beginnings of all demonstrations from experience §.202.
blocks.meier-para-320: If one wishes to find an intuitive judgment, then 1) let one take the thing that one senses as subject; 2) let one analyze the sensation, according to §.142. 257; 3) the marks discovered let one affirm of the subject §.319.
blocks.meier-para-321: The predicates of intuitive judgments can be contingent attributes, alterations, relations, effects, causes, actions and passions; but never the essence, the essential parts, the properties, and negative marks §.256. No negative judgment is an intuitive judgment, although it can be derived from an intuitive judgment, in that the marks that are opposed to those that we sense in the subject can with truth be denied of it §.295.
blocks.meier-para-322: From intuitive judgments universal ones are derived: 1) If one makes an intuitive judgment of all things of a species, according to §.320, and then infers that the predicate can be affirmed universally of the whole species §.263. 2) If one wishes to derive a universal judgment from One intuitive judgment, then a) let one seek the higher concept under which the subject belongs, according to §.259. b) Let one seek the condition of the intuitive judgment. c) Let one investigate whether it is absolutely necessary, or contingent, in the higher concept. In the latter case let one combine it with the subject, and then in both cases one can affirm the predicate universally of the higher concept §.299.
blocks.meier-para-323: Derivative judgments are demonstrated either from experience or from reason §.319. The former are mediate experiences §.203. 204. A judgment of experience is any judgment that is certain through experience, whether it be an intuitive judgment §.319, or a derivative judgment.
blocks.meier-para-324: Derivative judgments require either a shorter or a longer proof §.319. The former are called corollaries (consectarium, corollarium), and they can be either judgments of consideration or of practice §.312. They are for the most part adduced without proof, and easily found if one compares a few definitions, indemonstrable judgments and other truths with one another.
blocks.meier-para-325: Derivative judgments that require a longer proof (either from experience or from reason) are either judgments of consideration, or judgments of practice §.312. The former are called theorems (theorema), the latter however problems (problema).
blocks.meier-para-326: If one wishes to invent a theorem, then one must 1) invent the judgment, or it can already be known; 2) one must invent a longer proof, consequently a) one must seek out all proofs, whether they are already known to us, or one may learn them from others, or invent them anew; b) one must put them into a distinct connection, and c) one must understand the art of composing a proof from many proofs without causing confusion §.325.
blocks.meier-para-327: Whoever wishes to practice himself in the invention of theorems must begin with the easier ones, and with those that can be tested by experience, so that he may recognize his missteps the more easily.
blocks.meier-para-328: For the sake of distinctness, a problem is analysed into three parts: 1) The question (quaestio problematis) is the representation of the action that is to be done or left undone. Whenever we represent to ourselves a thing that can be regarded as an effect, a question can be raised. 2) The solution (solutio problematis) analyses the manner in which the question arises. It must therefore either cite all the actions of which the question consists, or all the causes, or both at once, and if one wants to find it, one must logically define the object of the question. 3) The proof of the problem (demonstratio problematis), which demonstrates that by observing the solution the question becomes actual. It accordingly presupposes the solution as a condition, and the whole problem can be regarded as a conditional theorem §.305. The test of the problem (proba, examen problematis) is that by which one is convinced that one has observed the solution.
blocks.meier-para-329: If one can discover no impossibility in the question, one may venture upon the solution, and one can invent it either through experience, or from reason and through abstraction, or in an arbitrary manner. If one wants to find it through experience, one must 1) seek to be present at the thing when it arises, and form for oneself through experience a distinct concept of the manner of its arising §.257. 2) One must observe precisely all the causes, and everything that takes place in the arising, namely when it falls within our senses. 3) The remaining causes, and the remaining parts of the arising, which do not fall within our senses, one must seek to guess at, by means of that part of erudition within whose scope the object belongs. 4) One compares the effect, whose manner of arising we cannot experience, with another that we can resolve through experience, and infers that the former arises in a similar manner and through similar causes.
blocks.meier-para-330: If one assumes an effect merely arbitrarily, 1) one must be well versed in those parts of erudition to which it belongs, form for oneself a distinct concept of it, and reflect upon all the powers and causes known to us, to see whether we may encounter something that belongs to the solution of the question. 2) If one connects many actions and causes arbitrarily with one another, and attends to what comes out, one also finds many solutions to many problems.
blocks.meier-para-331: In the midst of a system, through the pursuit of demonstrations from reason, one imperceptibly arrives at many solutions; and if one has already found the solutions of the lower questions, one need only separate out their differences, and one has the solution of the higher question, whether it speaks of an abstract action or of some other abstract effect.
blocks.meier-para-332: For the sake of the distinctness of the problem, one must find, from the distinct concepts of the effect and of the causes contained in the solution, what each cause contributes to the effect.
blocks.meier-para-333: To obtain brevity of the problems in a system, 1) one must resolve in the preceding ones the actions and effects of which the actions and effects of the following problems are composed; and 2) one must resolve in the preceding ones those actions and effects under which the questions of the following problems are contained.
blocks.meier-para-334: A problem is 1) true (veritas problematis), if it contains nothing impossible in itself, consequently if the solution is not contrary to the question; 2) complete (completum problema), if by the observation of the solution that follows which the question concerns; 3) exact (problema accuratum, adaequatum), if it contains neither too little nor too much in itself. And these are three perfections of problems.
blocks.meier-para-335: A problem is false, 1) if the solution is absolutely impossible; 2) if the solution is impossible in a certain respect, e.g. if it is not possible through the powers of human beings, or in certain circumstances; 3) if the solution can indeed become actual, but contributes nothing to the question; 4) if it even contradicts the question §.334.
blocks.meier-para-336: A problem is incomplete, 1) if the purpose is not attained by the most exact observation of the solution; 2) if one does not know how the solution can actually be made; 3) if the solution cannot be carried out in all cases where it is necessary §.334.
blocks.meier-para-337: A problem is not exact if it is indeed true and complete, but leads through detours, and contains too much in itself §.334.
blocks.meier-para-338: Occult qualities (qualitates occultae) are properties of which we have no clear and distinct cognition, and which we assume without sufficient ground. Since they conflict with the nature of learned cognition §.21. 168, whoever assumes them is either stupid or a deceiver. Consequently one must especially avoid them when one investigates the grounds of things, their nature and alterations, and hence also in the solution of problems.
blocks.meier-para-339: A borrowed judgment (lemma) is a provable judgment which is assumed in a system without proof, because with its proof it belongs to another system.
blocks.meier-para-340: Remarks (scholia) are judgments which in a system are neither proofs nor are proved, but which, for the sake of greater utility, have been mixed in among the rest.
blocks.meier-para-341: Equipollent judgments (iudicia aequipollentia) are different judgments in which the logical relation of one and the same subject and predicate is the same. E.g. not all human beings are virtuous, some human beings are not virtuous; not no human being is learned, some human beings are learned; everything has a ground, nothing is without ground. Since now the truth and incorrectness of a judgment are found in the logical relation §.295. 296, 1) all the remaining equipollent judgments are true if one is true; and 2) all the remaining ones are false if one is false. The equipollence of judgments depends on such alterations of the judgment as do not change its truth or incorrectness; otherwise they are not equipollent judgments.
blocks.meier-para-342: Judgments which have one and the same subject, predicate and quality, and among which only one is universal, contain one another in themselves (iudicia subalternata). The universal contains the others in itself (iudicium subalternans), and the rest are contained in it (iudicium subalternatum). E.g. all human beings can err, some human beings can err, one human being can err; no human being is sinless, some human beings are not sinless, one human being is not sinless. 1) If the universal judgment is true, then those contained in it are also true, but not conversely; 2) if the judgments contained in the universal are false, then the universal is also false, but not conversely §.302.
blocks.meier-para-343: Judgments contradict one another (iudicia contradictoria) when the one accurately denies what the other affirms. E.g. the judgments A and O, likewise E and I, contradict one another if they have one and the same subjects and predicates §.301. 341. Since every concept either belongs to every other concept or does not (for it cannot be thought at all that both at once or neither of the two could be the case), among all contradictory judgments either the affirmative is true and the negative false, or the negative true and the affirmative false §.295. Consequently one can infer 1) from the truth of the one among contradictory judgments to the incorrectness of the other; and 2) from the incorrectness of the one to the truth of the other.
blocks.meier-para-344: If one judgment affirms particularly what the other denies particularly, they are opposed to one another in a particular manner (iudicia subcontraria). Consequently the judgments I and O, if they have the same subjects and predicates. 1) These judgments can be true at the same time. For since their predicate can be a particular concept with respect to the subject §.262, it can be both affirmed and denied of it particularly with truth §.295. 2) These judgments can never both be false at the same time. For if I and O are false, then A and E are also false §.342. Consequently A and O, E and I, which have the same predicates and subjects, could be false at the same time, which is impossible §.343.
blocks.meier-para-345: If one judgment affirms universally what the other denies universally, consequently if A and E have the same subject and predicate, they are opposed to one another in a universal manner (iudicia contraria.) 1) These judgments can both be false.
