For their predicate can be a particular concept with respect to the subject §.262. Consequently it can be neither universally affirmed nor universally denied of it §.302. 2) These judgments cannot both be true. For if A and E were true, then I and O would also be true §.342. Consequently A and O, likewise E and I, although they had the same subject and predicate, could be true at the same time, and that is impossible §.343.
blocks.meier-para-346: That alteration by virtue of which the predicate is made out of the subject of a judgment, and the subject out of the predicate, is called the conversion of a judgment (conversio iudicii). The judgment with which the alteration takes place is called the converted one (iudicium conversum), and that which arises from it, the converting judgment (iudicium convertens). In conversion either the quantity of the judgment is changed, or not. In the first case the conversion occurs accidentally (conversio per accidens), in the other simply (conversio simplex). Insofar as a true judgment also remains true after the conversion, to that extent it can be converted (iudicium converti potest, iudicium reciprocabile).
blocks.meier-para-347: All affirmative judgments whose subject and predicate are reciprocal concepts can be converted simply, whether they be universal or singular judgments. For the subject also belongs to all contained under the predicate §.262. Consequently it can be universally affirmed of the predicate §.302. 346. E.g. the judgments which affirm the definition of the defined concept, and the members of the division, taken together under a disjunction, of the divided concept §.270. 287.
blocks.meier-para-348: All true particularly affirmative judgments can be converted simply. For the abstract concept of the subject belongs to some of those contained under it §.260, and can therefore be affirmed particularly of them §.295. And since the predicate belongs to some of those contained under the subject §.295, it can be assumed as their higher concept §.260 for the subject. Consequently the former subject can be affirmed particularly of the former predicate §.346.
blocks.meier-para-349: A universally negative judgment can be converted 1) simply. Otherwise the subject would not have to be contrary to all those contained under the predicate §.302, consequently it would have to belong to some of them §.343. Consequently the predicate would also have to belong to some of those contained under the subject §.348. Consequently the universally negative judgment would be false §.302, which is absurd; 2) accidentally. For since it can be converted simply, the particular judgment which is contained in the universal converting judgment is also true §.342, and through it the judgment is converted accidentally §.346.
blocks.meier-para-350: All universally affirmative judgments can be converted accidentally. For if they are true, the particularly affirmative judgments contained in them are also true §.342. These can be converted simply §.348, and precisely thereby the universal ones are converted accidentally §.346.
blocks.meier-para-351: If in the particularly negative judgments one sets the negation with the predicate, they become particularly affirmative judgments §.294, and can therefore then be converted simply §.348.
blocks.meier-para-352: A universally affirmative judgment is contraposed (contrapositio) when one changes its predicate into a negative concept, and universally denies the former subject of it. All true universally affirmative judgments can be contraposed, that is, to whatever the predicate does not belong, to that its subject also does not belong. Otherwise the predicate would have to be contrary to some things, and the subject belong to them §.343. One could therefore deny the predicate with truth of some of those contained under the subject §.295. Thus the universally affirmative judgment would be false §.302, and that is absurd. On learned inferences of reason.
blocks.meier-para-353: If some true judgments contain the sufficient ground of the truth of another, they are connected with one another §.15, and in this relation of true judgments consists the connection of truths (nexus veritatum).
blocks.meier-para-354: An inference of reason (ratiocinium) is a distinct representation of the connection of truths; which, if it is perfect in a higher degree, is called a learned or a logical inference of reason (ratiocinium logicum, eruditum).
blocks.meier-para-355: In an inference of reason we derive a truth from other truths §.353, 354. And since these other truths are therefore the proofs of the former §.191, we make an inference of reason when we distinctly derive a truth from its proofs. Consequently the distinct representation of the consequence of a proof is an inference of reason §.191.
blocks.meier-para-356: That judgment which is derived from others in an inference of reason is the conclusion (conclusio, probandum, principiatum). But those judgments from which the conclusion is derived are the premises (praemissae, data, sumtiones, principia).
blocks.meier-para-357: The subjects and predicates of the judgments of which an inference of reason consists are called the principal concepts of an inference of reason (termini). The subject of the conclusion is the smaller principal concept (terminus minor), but its predicate the greater principal concept (terminus maior). The principal concept which, besides the smaller and greater, is found in the premises, is called the middle principal concept (terminus medius).
blocks.meier-para-358: Since the premises contain the proof of the conclusion §.355.356, but in them, besides the parts of the conclusion, nothing further is contained than the middle principal concept §.357; the latter is the proof §.191, consequently the condition of the conclusion §.297. One therefore finds the middle principal concept following the guidance of the 297th and 298th paragraphs; and an inference of reason consists in this, that we derive a judgment from its condition in a distinct manner §.355.
blocks.meier-para-359: The matter of the inference of reason (ratiocinii materia) consists in its premises, but its form (ratiocinii forma) in the consequence of the conclusion from the premises.
blocks.meier-para-360: A correct inference of reason (ratiocinium verum) must be correct in the matter as well as in the form §.359.355. 193. If therefore either the matter is false, or the form, or both at the same time, it is a false, incorrect inference of reason (ratiocinium falsum). An erroneous inference of reason (ratiocinium erroneum) is a false inference of reason insofar as it is held to be a correct one §.109. From §.193 and 194 it is evident when an inference of reason has demonstrative certainty, or not.
blocks.meier-para-361: Because the consequence in every inference of reason must be distinct §.355, but no distinctness is possible without order §.142, the judgments of an inference of reason must be duly ordered together. Since now no order is possible without rules, certain rules of inference are necessary, according to which an inference of reason must be arranged if it is to have a correct and distinct consequence.
blocks.meier-para-362: It is impossible that something be and not be at the same time. Or, if one and the same thing is affirmed or denied of a thing at the same time, it is nothing. This proposition is called the principle of contradiction (principium contradictionis), and it is the first internal mark of truth §.95, on which all consequences of inferences of reason must rest if they are to be true §.361.
blocks.meier-para-363: What can be universally affirmed or denied with truth of a concept can also be affirmed or denied with truth of any other concept whatever that belongs under it §.342. Otherwise two contradictory judgments would have to be true at the same time §.343, and that is contrary to the principle of contradiction §.362. This proposition is called the inference from the universal to the particular (dictum de omni et nullo).
blocks.meier-para-364: If the sufficient ground is true, its consequence is also true; otherwise the sufficient ground would not be a sufficient ground §.15, which is contrary to §.362. Consequently, if the consequence is false, the sufficient ground is also false, because otherwise the sufficient ground could be without consequence. This inference is called the inference from the sufficient ground to its consequence (a ratione sufficiente ad rationatum valet consequentia).
blocks.meier-para-365: If one of contradictory judgments is true, the other is false; and if the one is false, the other is true §.343.362. This proposition is called: the inference from the opposite (ab uno oppositorum ad alterum valet consequentia).
blocks.meier-para-366: If a judgment is true, then that which has arisen through a logical alteration of the first, which can be undertaken without prejudice to truth, must also be true. Otherwise the logical alteration would have to be prejudicial to truth and not prejudicial, which is impossible §.362. This inference is called: the inference from the logical alteration of a true judgment.
blocks.meier-para-367: An ordinary inference of reason (ratiocinium ordinarium) is an inference of reason in which one infers from the universal to the particular §.363. For example: all virtues contribute something to my happiness; now all philosophical virtues are virtues, therefore all philosophical virtues contribute something to my happiness. All other inferences of reason are extraordinary inferences of reason (ratiocinium extraordinarium).
blocks.meier-para-368: All ordinary inferences of reason have two premises which have the middle principal concept in common with one another §.367. That premise in them which contains the greater principal concept is called the major premise of ordinary inferences of reason (propositio maior ratiociniorum ordinariorum); but that which contains the smaller principal concept, the minor premise of the same (propositio minor).
blocks.meier-para-369: That species of ordinary inferences of reason in which the middle principal concept stands in the subject of the major premise and in the predicate of the minor premise is called the first figure (figura prima ratiociniorum). For example: all human beings can err; the learned are human beings, therefore the learned can err. In this figure the minor premise and the conclusion have one subject §.368. Consequently these two judgments always have the same quantity §.301.
blocks.meier-para-370: That species of ordinary inferences of reason in which the middle principal concept stands in the predicate of both premises is called the second figure (figura secunda). E.g. no absurd thing is true, everything that stands in the Bible is true; therefore nothing that stands in the Bible is absurd.
blocks.meier-para-371: That species of ordinary inferences of reason in which the middle principal concept stands in the subject of both premises is called the third figure (figura tertia). For example: all the learned have an improved understanding, some of the learned are vicious; therefore some of the vicious have an improved understanding.
blocks.meier-para-372: That species of ordinary inferences of reason in which the middle principal concept stands in the predicate of the major premise, and in the subject of the minor premise, is called the fourth, or the Galenic figure (figura quarta, galenica). For example: no stupid human being is learned, some of the learned are pious; therefore some of the pious are not stupid people.
blocks.meier-para-373: The figures of inferences of reason (figurae ratiociniorum) are accordingly different species of ordinary inferences of reason, which arise from the different arrangement of the middle principal concept with the remaining principal concepts in the premises; and there are no more than four figures §.369. 372.
blocks.meier-para-374: From the inference from the universal to the particular §.363, the following rules of all ordinary inferences of reason flow: 1) In an ordinary inference of reason there can be neither more nor fewer principal concepts contained than three. Such an inference contains only three judgments, consequently only six places for the principal concepts §.368.357. Now it contains 1) a principal concept of which something is universally affirmed or denied, and of which it is said in the other premise that another concept belongs to it. It therefore occurs twice, because it is the middle principal concept §.368. 2) The smaller principal concept occurs in the conclusion and the minor premise §.357. 368; and 3) the greater principal concept in the conclusion and the major premise §.357. 368.
blocks.meier-para-375: 2) The middle principal concept must not be put into the conclusion. For in ordinary inferences of reason the greater principal concept is affirmed or denied of the smaller in the conclusion, because according to the statement of the premises the smaller principal concept belongs to the middle one, of which the greater can be affirmed or denied §.364. Consequently the conclusion can consist only of the smaller and greater principal concepts.
blocks.meier-para-376: 3) The premises must not all deny, for one must affirm that the smaller or greater principal concept is connected with the middle one §.363, or from purely negative premises nothing follows, although from purely affirmative ones something follows. If the middle principal concept is a negative concept, at least one premise is merely infinite §.294, and then it merely seems as if all the premises denied.
blocks.meier-para-377: 4) The premises must not all be particular judgments; otherwise one would not be inferring from the universal to the particular §.363, or from purely particular premises nothing follows, although from purely universal ones something can follow.
blocks.meier-para-378: 5) If one premise denies, the conclusion must also deny: for then the inference of reason is directed by the negative part of the inference from the universal to the particular §.363, and it must therefore have a negative conclusion.
blocks.meier-para-379: 6) If one premise is a particular judgment, the conclusion must also be a particular one; for then one infers: because some things of a kind belong to that concept of which something is universally affirmed or denied, this can also be affirmed or denied of those some §.363.
blocks.meier-para-380: 7) The conclusion is always directed by the weaker part of the inference of reason: for the negative and particular premises are called the weaker part of the inference of reason (pars ratiocinii debilior) §.378. 379.
blocks.meier-para-381: 8) In the conclusion there must not be contained less than in the premises. For otherwise the smaller and greater principal concepts would contain less in themselves in the conclusion than in the premises, and more than three principal concepts would therefore be found in the inference of reason §.374.
blocks.meier-para-382: 9) In the conclusion there must not be contained more than in the premises. Otherwise the smaller and greater principal concepts would contain more in the conclusion than in the premises, and there would therefore be more than three principal concepts in the inference of reason §.374.
blocks.meier-para-383: Besides these rules, two further rules must be observed in the first figure: 1) The minor premise must always affirm in the first figure. For since it has as its subject the subject of the conclusion §.369, it affirms of it that it belongs to the middle principal concept §.363. If the middle principal concept is negative, the minor premise is infinite §.376, and so nevertheless an affirmative judgment §.294.
blocks.meier-para-384: 2) The major premise must always be universal in the first figure. For if the conclusion is universal, the major premise can only be universal §.379; but if it is a particular judgment, the minor premise is also of that kind §.369, and so the major premise must once again be universal §.377. Because singular judgments belong to the universal ones §.301, they make no exception to the rules which demand the universality of the judgments of an inference of reason.
blocks.meier-para-385: The moods of ordinary inferences of reason (modi ratiociniorum ordinariorum) are different species of inferences of reason of one figure, which arise from the different quality and quantity of the judgments of an inference of reason.
blocks.meier-para-386: If the conclusion in the first figure affirms universally, then the minor premise also affirms §.383. 378 and universally §.379. 369, and the major premise must also affirm §.378 and be universal §.384. 379. The mood of inferences of reason in the first figure whose conclusion affirms universally is called Barbara, e.g. all truths are useful, all philosophical truths are truths; therefore all philosophical truths are useful.
blocks.meier-para-387: If the conclusion in the first figure denies universally, the minor premise must affirm §.383, and universally §.369. 379, and the major premise must deny §.380, and universally §.384. 379. The mood of inferences of reason in the first figure which have a universally negative conclusion is called Celarent, e.g. no vice makes me more perfect, all pride is a vice; therefore no pride makes me more perfect.
blocks.meier-para-388: If the conclusion in the first figure affirms particularly, the minor premise must affirm §.383. 378, and particularly §.369. 380, and the major premise must affirm §.378, and universally §.384. 377. The mood of inferences of reason in the first figure whose conclusion affirms particularly is called Darii, e.g. all persistent unbelievers are damned, some of the learned are persistent unbelievers; therefore some of the learned are damned.
blocks.meier-para-389: If the conclusion in the first figure denies particularly, the minor premise must affirm §.383, and particularly §.369, and the major premise must deny §.380, and universally §.384. 377. The mood of inferences of reason in the first figure whose conclusion denies particularly is called Ferio; e.g. no good action is punished by GOD, some mere natural works of human beings are good actions; therefore some mere natural works of human beings are not punished by GOD. In the first figure only four moods of inferences of reason are possible §.385-388.
blocks.meier-para-390: All true judgments which can be conclusions in ordinary inferences of reason are either A or E, or I or O §.301. Consequently, in the first figure all these judgments can be concluded §.386-389, and for this reason it is called a perfect figure. Hence the remaining figures are not necessary.
blocks.meier-para-391: If, contrary to the rules so far, one makes inferences of reason whose premises and conclusions are correct, the latter do not follow from the former necessarily, but are only accidentally true. Such inferences are therefore no objections against the correctness of these rules.
blocks.meier-para-392: A conditional inference of reason (ratiocinium hypotheticum, conditionale, connexum) is an inference of reason which infers from the sufficient ground to the consequence §.364. Since now in no kind of judgments is the consequence of a judgment affirmed from its condition except in the conditional ones §.305, these inferences of reason have a conditional premise, which is called their major premise. It must have a correct consequence §.306, otherwise one infers from the stick in the corner (argumentum a baculo ad angulum).
blocks.meier-para-393: In a conditional inference of reason one infers either 1) from the correctness of the former to the correctness of the latter §.364. 305. Then the minor premise affirms that the first is true, and the conclusion that the last is true (modus ratiociniorum hypotheticorum ponens). For example: if there is a providence of GOD, all anxious cares are in vain: now the first is true, therefore also the last; Or 2) from the incorrectness of the latter to the incorrectness of the former §.364. 305. Then the minor premise affirms the incorrectness of the latter, and the conclusion the incorrectness of the former (modus ratiociniorum hypotheticorum tollens), e.g. if there is a blind fate, there are no free actions; now the last is false, therefore also the first.
blocks.meier-para-394: Because a thing can have several sufficient grounds, one cannot in conditional inferences of reason infer always from the incorrectness of the first to the incorrectness of the last, nor from the correctness of the last to the correctness of the first §.305.
blocks.meier-para-395: Disjunctive inferences of reason (ratiocinium disiunctivum) are inferences of reason which infer from one opposite to the other §.365. Consequently they contain a disjunctive premise, which is called their major premise §.307. If this is contrary to one of the rules proved in §.308, it has no consequence, and the disjunctive inference of reason is incorrect in form §.360.
blocks.meier-para-396: In disjunctive inferences of reason one infers either 1) from the correctness of one member of the disjunction to the incorrectness of the rest §.395. 365. Then the minor premise must declare one member to be true, and the conclusion the rest to be false (modus ratiociniorum disiunctivorum ponendo tollens). E.g. matter can either think or not, now the latter is true, therefore the first is false; or 2) from the incorrectness of all members except one to the correctness of this one §.395. 365. Then in the minor premise it must be affirmed of all members except one that they are false, and in the conclusion of this one that it is true (modus ratiociniorum disiunctivorum tollendo ponens). For example: matter can either think or not; now the first is false, therefore the other is true.
blocks.meier-para-397: A dilemma (ratiocinium cornutum, crocodillinum, dilemma, trilemma etc.) is a conditional inference of reason whose latter part is a disjunctive judgment in which all members are false. The conditional judgment whose latter part is disjunctive is the major premise; the minor premise affirms that the latter is false in its entirety, and the conclusion affirms that the first is false. A dilemma must therefore conform at the same time to the rules of conditional and of disjunctive inferences of reason §.392. 393. 395. For example: if this world were not the best, then either no best world would be possible, or GOD would have had no cognition of it, or he would not have been able to create it, or he would not have been willing to create it; now the last is false in its entirety, therefore also the first.
blocks.meier-para-398: The inferences of reason which infer from the logical alteration of a judgment to the judgment arisen through the alteration are called immediate inferences (consequentia immediata) §.366. For example: all human beings can err, therefore some human beings can also err; or, there is a GOD, therefore it is false that there is no GOD.
blocks.meier-para-399: An inference of reason is either so constituted that its correct form is manifest, or it is hidden: the former is a formal inference of reason (ratiocinium formale), the latter however a hidden one (ratiocinium crypticum), which can therefore seem to be incorrect in form. In order to conceal the logical art, and to avoid pedantry, hidden inferences of reason are to be recommended.
blocks.meier-para-400: To the hidden inferences of reason belong chiefly the mutilated inferences of reason (enthymema), in which a judgment is omitted, that is, is not thought as distinctly as the rest, because it is entirely certain and so familiar to someone that it occurs to him at once. E.g. all human beings can err, therefore I too can err.
blocks.meier-para-401: To the mutilated inferences of reason belong 1) the contracted inferences of reason (ratiocinium contractum), when one adds merely the middle principal concept to the conclusion, yet in such a way that it does not become a conditional judgment. For example: this world is the best, because it has been chosen by GOD. 2) The inferences by analysis (inductio), which lay down the following major premise as a ground, but omit it: what can be affirmed or denied of every lower concept can be universally affirmed or denied of their higher concept §.263. If in the minor premise all lower concepts are cited, it is a complete inference by analysis (inductio completa). For example: the first person of the Godhead is GOD, the second also, the third also; therefore all persons of the Godhead are GOD. 3) The inferences by example (exemplum in ratiociniis), when one affirms or denies, of another lower concept which belongs to the same higher concept, that which one affirms or denies of a lower concept for the sake of its higher concept. For example: human beings can sin, therefore all holy angels can also sin.
blocks.meier-para-402: An inference of reason which is incorrect in form (paralogismus), when its fault is hidden, is called a fallacy (sophisma, fallacia, captio).
blocks.meier-para-403: A fallacy can arise: 1) if we connect separated things in an incorrect manner, and separate connected things in an incorrect manner (sophisma sensus compositi et divisi). For example: where there are three thalers, there are two thalers; now three and two thalers make five thalers, therefore where there are three thalers, there are five thalers. 2) If a principal concept is taken in a twofold manner (sophisma figurae dictionis). For example: a philosopher is a species of the learned, Leibniz is a philosopher, therefore Leibniz is a species of the learned.
blocks.meier-para-404: 3) If one takes a principal concept once with a restriction and the other time without restriction (fallacia accidentis, seu a dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter, aut vice versa). E.g. whoever says you are an animal speaks the truth; now whoever says you are an ass says you are an animal, therefore he speaks the truth. 4) If one assumes a wrong middle principal concept (fallacia medii). E.g. whoever looks pale studies diligently; now Caius looks pale, therefore he studies diligently.
blocks.meier-para-405: 5) If one takes the judgment which one has proved for that which one was to prove (sophisma heterozeteseos). For example: if one is to prove the immortality of the soul, and one proves its incorruptibility. 6) If one takes the judgment which one has refuted for that which one was to refute (sophisma ignorationis elenchi). E.g. if, against him who asserts that the soul can die, one proves that it lives eternally. 7) If a composite judgment is regarded merely as a simple one in an inference of reason (sophisma polyzeteseos). E.g. it is either true that dogs alone among all four-footed animals have reason, or it is not true; if the first, dogs have reason, if the last, all four-footed animals have reason.
blocks.meier-para-406: An inference of reason consists either of several inferences of reason, or of only one. The latter is a simple inference of reason (ratiocinium simplex, probatio simplex), the former however a composite inference of reason (ratiocinium compositum). If an inference of reason is composite, the several inferences of reason of which it consists are either connected or not §.353. In the latter case it is a ratiocinium copulatum, e.g. all spirits are immortal, GOD and all human souls are spirits, therefore they are immortal. In the former case the premise of the one is the conclusion of the other, and it is called a series of connected inferences of reason (ratiocinatio polysyllogistica, probatio composita). For example: what accords with the laws of nature makes me more perfect, virtue accords with the laws of nature, therefore virtue makes me more perfect; that which makes me more perfect, to that I am obligated, virtue makes me more perfect, therefore I am obligated to it.
blocks.meier-para-407: In a series of connected inferences of reason there occur not only some whose conclusions are premises of others, but also such whose premises are conclusions of others §.406. The former are called prosyllogisms (prosyllogismus), and the latter episyllogisms (episyllogismus). And some judgments occur twice in such a series §.406.
blocks.meier-para-408: In order to avoid all confusion in a long series of connected inferences of reason, 1) one divides a long proof into many parts, by proving separately the chief premises as particular theorems. 2) One does not connect with one another purely ordinary and formal inferences of reason. 3) One proves either only the major premises of the prosyllogisms, or only their minor premises. 4) One derives the conclusions from contracted inferences of reason §.401 (epicherema). 5) One omits all judgments that occur twice §.407, and that is called a heaped inference of reason (sorites). E.g. youth accords with the laws of nature, what accords with the laws of nature, that makes me more perfect, what makes me more perfect, to that I am obligated; therefore I am obligated to virtue.
blocks.meier-para-409: If the inferences of reason of which the heaped inference of reason consists are of the first figure, and the minor premises of the episyllogisms are omitted, it is a common heaped inference of reason (sorites communis). E.g. the example cited just above. But if it consists of purely conditional premises, it is called a conditional one (sorites hypotheticus). E.g. if the human being has a limited understanding, he has confused representations; if he has confused representations, he can err; if he can err, he can sin: therefore, if the human being has a limited understanding, he can sin.
blocks.meier-para-410: If in a series of connected inferences of reason one or more judgments are omitted, a leap in the proof is committed (saltus in probando). The omitted judgments are either certain to him who is to be convinced by the proof, and occur to him easily; or not. In the first case the leap is legitimate (saltus legitimus), in the other however illegitimate (saltus illegitimus).
blocks.meier-para-411: If a conclusion is derived from premises which are just as uncertain as it itself, the proofs are begged (petitio principii seu quaesiti.) But if a conclusion is assumed as its own premise, this fault is called the return in the proof (circulus in probando).
blocks.meier-para-412: A proof proves too little (probatio minus probans) if the whole conclusion does not become certain through it; but if something follows from a proof besides the conclusion which is false or even too different from the conclusion, it proves too much (probatio plus probans).
blocks.meier-para-413: Through inferences of reason one can 1) attain the most distinct certainty that is possible to a human being §.355. 2) Resist errors most easily; 3) discover new truths; and 4) discover all proofs that are necessary in order to erect a learned system, etc. On the method of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-414: Method (methodus) is a more noticeable or greater order of thoughts. Insofar as several thoughts are together in one and the same manner, or follow upon one another, to that extent there is an order among them, which arises when different thoughts are coordinated with one another according to one and the same rules.
blocks.meier-para-415: Method is, in cognition §.414. 11, and so is either an order of common cognition, the common method (methodus vulgaris), or of rational cognition §.17. 18, the rational method (methodus rationalis). To the former belongs the aesthetic method §.19, to the latter, however, the learned method (methodus erudita, logica, philosophica), the method of learned cognition §.21.
blocks.meier-para-416: The learned method promotes 1) the distinctness of learned cognition §.142 n. 4. 2) Truth in a system and thoroughness §.105. 3) The unity and thoroughgoing connection of a system. 4) The perfection of learned cognition: for all order is a perfection. 5) The retention of truths by memory §.414.
blocks.meier-para-417: The more thoughts are connected with one another, and the more and the more important common rules according to which this connection takes place, the greater and more perfect is the method §.414. Consequently, for the greatest perfection of a learned cognition it is required that it be as methodical as possible §.416.
blocks.meier-para-418: A method connects thoughts either according to only a single common rule, or according to several. The former is a simple method (methodus simplex), the latter, however, a composite method (methodus composita). The latter is more perfect than the former §.417.
blocks.meier-para-419: The difference of methods derives from the difference of the rules according to which the thoughts are coordinated with one another §.414, and the difference of the rules flows from the difference of the cognitive faculties, and from the different constitution of the cognition that is to be thought according to a method.
blocks.meier-para-420: Since learned cognition is a distinct cognition from grounds §.21. 17, the thoughts in the learned method must follow upon one another in such a way that their connection thereby becomes distinctly certain §.415. 419. This is the fundamental law of the learned method.
blocks.meier-para-421: The method of dogmatic truths is different from the method of historical ones §.419. 104. In the former the thoughts must be proved from one another, either through a demonstration or through an insufficient proof §.191. If the first is the case, it is called a demonstrative or scientific method (methodus demonstrativa, scientifica, apodictica).
blocks.meier-para-422: In the learned method of dogmatic truths, only thoughts are coordinated with one another that are either the grounds of the truth, distinctness and certainty of others, or the consequences, or both at once §.421. 420.15. Thus the grounds are either put before the consequences or placed after them. The former is the synthetic method (methodus synthetica), the latter, however, the analytic method (methodus analytica). Consequently the learned method is either synthetic or analytic, whether it be demonstrative or not §.421.
blocks.meier-para-423: The analytic method is very inconvenient if one wants to treat or learn an extensive system according to it. But it is very well suited 1) when one wants to draw up an outline for a system, in order afterwards to treat it according to the synthetic method; 2) when one wants to discover, from the consequences and conclusions, the grounds and premises; 3) when one wants to repeat a system already learned often; 4) when one wants to think through properly the individual shorter parts of a system §.422.
blocks.meier-para-424: The synthetic method is always attended with many inconveniences if one makes use of it in such cases where the analytic has been recommended §.423. But it has great advantages if one makes use of it: 1) when one wants to think through and treat a system already discovered, considered as a whole; 2) when one wants to learn it; 3) when one wants to discover the consequences and conclusions from the grounds and premises §.422.
blocks.meier-para-425: In the synthetic method the grounds must always be thought before the consequences §.422. Consequently 1) the concepts that are marks of other concepts must be explained before the others §.115, and thus the higher before the lower §.261. 2) The unprovable truths must precede the provable ones §.314-317. 3) The premises must be thought before the conclusions §.356, and thus the prosyllogisms before the episyllogisms §.407. 4) Those provable truths from which others follow must precede these. In the analytic method everything stands the reverse way §.422.
blocks.meier-para-426: The synthetic method, which has merely the aim of promoting the mathematical certainty of cognition §.161, is called the mathematical method (methodus mathematica). It must therefore not only conform most exactly to the rules of the synthetic §.425, but by virtue of them one also either omits everything that is not indispensably required for mathematical certainty, or puts it into remarks §.340. It is of great use in very difficult demonstrations, especially for beginners, but if one accustoms oneself to it alone, one acquires a merely learned cognition §.161, and it is accordingly not to be advised §.40.
blocks.meier-para-427: Art (ars) is a sum of rules that are thought according to an order. The artificial method (methodus artificialis, scholae) is the method insofar as it is learned and practiced through art. The natural method (methodus naturalis) is the method insofar as it is not artificial, but follows from the nature of the cognition and of him who thinks. The mixed method (methodus mixta) is the natural method insofar as the artificial comes to its aid.
blocks.meier-para-428: Among the artificial learned methods the best are 1) the inferential method (methodus syllogistica), when one analyzes all proofs into nothing but formal inferences, and commits no leaps. It does a beginner good service. Otherwise it is too extensive, too tedious and not distinct enough. 2) The method by tables (methodus tabellaris), when one arranges together all the members of the divisions and parts of the whole so that it becomes evident to what higher concept and whole each thought belongs. It promotes the distinct concept of an entire system, and memory; but it often falls into the forced, attention is overburdened, and thoroughness cannot be properly attained through it. 3) The method according to a partition of an entire system, when one lets the judgments follow one another according to the difference of their subjects; hence chapters, sections, etc. arise. When it is combined with the synthetic, it does not hinder thoroughness, and provides the benefit of the method by tables.
blocks.meier-para-429: If one wants to treat a system, this must be done according to the synthetic, and in some cases according to the analytic method §.423. 424, for they suit the nature of a system §.420. Now whatever of all the remaining artificial methods can be combined with it, whether to promote distinctness and certainty, or memory, or to increase order, that one should connect with the synthetic and analytic method. Consequently, affectation in method (affectatio in methodo) is a fault 1) when the artificial method is good for nothing, is contrary to nature, and is wholly arbitrary. 2) When one binds oneself too exactly to a simple method, and will never make an exception from it. 3) When one observes the rules of method far too exactly and anxiously.
blocks.meier-para-430: The learned method must be natural and unaffected §.429. It must therefore conform to the nature of learned cognition, and be observed without anxious effort. Consequently it must conform to the head of him who wants to think according to it. Whoever has the gift for it can therefore make use 1) of the Socratic method (methodus socratica), by virtue of which the thoughts follow upon one another as they occasion one another, as questions and answers in the conversation of several persons; 2) of the Platonic method (methodus platonica), by virtue of which the thoughts follow upon one another as in a free speech, so that all kinds of learned thoughts are mixed together, without one's making formal and manifest inferences.
blocks.meier-para-431: If one wants to treat a system according to the synthetic method, one must 1) lay only One truth at the foundation, from which everything else is derived, so that the system obtains a unity and a thoroughgoing connection, so that it contains neither more nor less than is necessary. 2) One lays a partition at the foundation, and divides the system into several sections, yet in such a way that no exception from the synthetic method is thereby made. 3) The learned thoughts themselves must follow upon one another as follows. a) First come the definitions; b) then follow either the unprovable truths or the intuitive judgments; c) then the provable truths. d) The corollaries and remarks are scattered throughout, wherever they are necessary and useful §.420. 425.
blocks.meier-para-432: The method of historical truth §.421 must conform to the nature of historical truths §.419; consequently one must think them in the order in which their objects are connected with one another either according to space or time. To this belongs, then, the chronological method (methodus chronologica), when one thinks the events in just the sequence in which they actually followed upon one another; and the geographical method (methodus geographica), by virtue of which one thinks the events that happen, or have happened, in a place according to the chronological method. Since the actual events of the world also cohere, and a human being can often see this connection, one can, at least often, also make use of the rational method in the case of historical truths §.415.
blocks.meier-para-433: The best learned composite method can seem a disorder to a human being who does not know its rules, or who has accustomed himself to another method, or only to a simple one. But for that reason no well-founded reproach can be made against such a method.
blocks.meier-para-434: A doctrine (doctrina) is a sum of dogmatic truths that have one and the same object. A discipline (disciplina) is a doctrine insofar as it is cognized methodically. A demonstrated discipline is a science (scientia obiective spectata). Learned cognition is always at the beginning a doctrine, then one gives it the shape of a discipline, and finally the shape of a science, and then it has attained its greatest perfection.
blocks.meier-para-435: Whoever thinks, thinks either according to a method or according to none §.414. The former thinks methodically (methodice cogitare, methodicum, acroamaticum, disciplinale in cognitione), the latter, however, tumultuarily (tumultuaria cognitio). No tumultuary cognition can be properly learned §.416.
blocks.meier-para-436: Meditating (meditatio) is that occupation of our cognitive faculties through which we reflect on a thing according to the rules of a method. If it takes place according to the rules of the learned method, it is a learned meditating (meditatio erudita), which is as manifold as there are different kinds of the learned method. Without this learned meditating we cannot attain any learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-437: Whoever wants to meditate in a learned way 1) let him choose an object to which he directs his attention; 2) let him think, one after another, the marks of it, which make up its definition, the unprovable, and finally the provable predicates of it. These one has either already learned, and then one does well to write while meditating; or one wants to learn them, and then one must read in a book, or listen to oral presentation; or one wants first to discover them. 3) One should examine whether what one thinks is a concept, a judgment, a theorem, etc., and consider it until one has satisfied all the rules that logic prescribes for each kind of learned thoughts.
blocks.meier-para-438: It is a disgrace when, out of pedantry, one despises all ways of thinking that are not cut over the last of that method with which one has fallen in love, and when, like a charlatan, one makes too much ado of the method one loves. On the learned presentation. On the use of words.
blocks.meier-para-439: Logical characteristic (logica characteristica heuristica) is the science of the rules that one must observe if one wants to designate learned cognition in a skilful way. Logical interpretation (hermeneutica logica) is the science of the rules for how one is to cognize, in a learned way, the things designated from the signs.
blocks.meier-para-440: A sign (signum, symbolum) is a means by whose use the actuality of another thing can be cognized, which other thing is called the thing designated or the meaning (signatum, significatus). An expression (terminus) is a sign of cognition; the expressions that ordinarily consist in a human voice are called words (vocabulum). The cognition designated through the expressions and words is called their meaning (significatus vocabuli et termini).
blocks.meier-para-441: That meaning which he who uses the word wants to designate by the word is the true meaning (significatus hermeneutice verus). Every other meaning, however, is the false (significatus hermeneutice falsus). The true meaning can be a false concept, and the false a true concept.
blocks.meier-para-442: Discourse (oratio) is a series of words that designates representations that are connected with one another. The series of representations is called the sense of the discourse (sensus orationis), which is either a true sense (sensus hermeneutice verus), if the speaker wanted to designate it, or a false (sensus hermeneutice falsus), if it is not the true. Presentation (propositio) is the production of a cognition in others by means of a discourse, whether it be an oral or a written presentation.
blocks.meier-para-443: As many kinds of cognition as there are, so many kinds of discourse and of presentation there are also §.442. There are therefore common discourses, aesthetic discourses, rational discourses, and likewise such kinds of presentation §.17. 18.19. A learned discourse (oratio erudita) is a discourse whose sense is a learned cognition §.21, and we present something in a learned way (erudite proponere) when, through a learned discourse, we produce a learned cognition in others.
blocks.meier-para-444: The learned discourse must, together with all its parts, be so constituted that the highest perfection of learned cognition is not hindered, but promoted and designated §.442. One must therefore observe in it 1) all aesthetic rules of discourse that are not contrary to the logical perfection of cognition §.34. 2) Avoid all aesthetic perfections that are contrary to the required logical perfection of discourse §.34.
blocks.meier-para-445: A discourse is either merely learned (oratio mere erudita), if it designates nothing further than a merely learned cognition, but in the opposite case it is not a merely learned discourse (oratio non mere erudita). And likewise the learned presentation is different §.443. The latter are the best §.40. 32.
blocks.meier-para-446: The learned expression must be extensive §.25. 444. Consequently 1) a scholar must know as many expressions as are required to designate all his learned thoughts. 2) One must know all the necessary technical terms of one's main science, and in case of need it is permitted to invent new expressions. A technical term (terminus technicus) is an expression that may not be used at all outside an art or discipline. 3) One must know all expressions of equal meaning (synonyma), or all expressions that signify one and the same. 4) The learned expression must designate everything that one thinks, and designate neither more nor less than one wants to say. 5) One must know all meanings of an expression that it has already received through common and learned usage of speaking. The common usage of speaking (usus loquendi) is the agreement in common life by virtue of which people who speak a language connect one or more meanings with certain words. The learned usage of speaking (receptus terminorum significatus) is just such an agreement of those who apply themselves to a discipline.
blocks.meier-para-447: The learned expression must be great, important and decorous enough for learned cognition §.444. 26. Consequently one must avoid in learned presentation all base, ridiculous and vulgar expressions that are in use only among the rabble.
blocks.meier-para-448: The learned expression must be correct §.444. 27. A true expression (terminus verus) must correctly designate its true meaning §.441: an expression that is not true is a false expression (terminus falsus).
blocks.meier-para-449: An expression is false: 1) if its meaning is a false concept, and he who uses the expression is convinced of the incorrectness of the meaning; 2) if we believe we understand an expression when we nevertheless do not understand it; such a false expression is an empty expression, or an empty word (terminus inanis). We understand an expression (terminum intelligere) when we cognize its meaning from it. An empty word arises: a) when we take the concept of the word itself for its meaning §.440. b) When the meaning of the word is an erroneous or deceptive concept (conceptus deceptor), a concept that we believe we have, when we nevertheless have none. 3) When it does not correctly designate a true concept §.448.
blocks.meier-para-450: A familiar expression (terminus familiaris) is an expression that we have grown accustomed to, or that we believe we understand, although we do not understand it, because we do not attend to its meaning. Such expressions can be true expressions, but in using them we stand in the greatest danger of hatching empty expressions, if we connect with one another a pair of familiar expressions whose meanings are impossible or contradict one another §.449. Hence people can speak of nothing and yet seem to understand one another, namely if they use expressions that are familiar to them.
blocks.meier-para-451: Although in learned discourses one cannot avoid the false expressions of the first kind §.449 when one must refute errors; one must nevertheless avoid all other false and empty expressions, because thoughtlessness and errors arise from their use. To that end one must use no expression 1) whose meaning one has not cognized, and 2) whose meaning one has not examined as to whether it is a true or false concept.
blocks.meier-para-452: A coarse expression (terminus crassus) is an expression whose meaning is a coarse cognition §.102. The use of empty expressions in learned discourses is the word-mongering of scholars, in which one sells words for things. E.g. if a scholar is to give the ground of a thing, and he has designated the thing with an expression that he afterwards adduces as the ground, he sells words for things. All this one must avoid §.451.
blocks.meier-para-453: The learned expression must be clear §.444. 28. One must therefore not only be able to distinguish it properly from other expressions oneself, but its meaning must also be sufficiently clear. An obscure expression (terminus obscurus) has an obscure meaning, a clear one (terminus clarus) a clear one, etc. An obscure expression is for that reason not an empty one §.449, and an expression that is obscure to me is for that reason not absolutely obscure also to other people §.126.
blocks.meier-para-454: From an expression its meaning can either be clearly cognized or not. The former is an intelligible expression (terminus intelligibilis), the latter, however, an unintelligible expression (terminus non intelligibilis). Although in a learned discourse one cannot use nothing but expressions that are intelligible to all people; one must nevertheless use nothing but such expressions as can be intelligible even to people of mediocre understanding, who have a mediocre command of the language, if they pay only mediocre attention to the discourse §.453.
blocks.meier-para-455: Whoever wants to make use of the most intelligible expressions in a learned discourse §.454, 1) must prefer the better-known and more usual expressions to the less known and less usual, if they are otherwise equal to one another. 2) He must always connect with the expression that meaning which is connected with it by the usage of speaking, in common life as well as in the disciplines §.446, until necessity forces him to the contrary; 3) he must, if the usage of speaking is manifold, connect with the expressions the most usual meanings (significatus famosissimus), that is, those that are connected with the expression by most people in most cases; 4) if in a certain case the three preceding rules do not suffice, then one should explain that meaning in which one takes an expression §.268.
blocks.meier-para-456: The learned expression must be certain §.444. 29. A certain expression (terminus certus) is so constituted that one knows not only for certain that it has a meaning, but also that it has precisely this and no other meaning. An expression is uncertain (terminus incertus) if it is not certain; and through the use of uncertain expressions the discourse is put on screws.
blocks.meier-para-457: An ambiguous expression (terminus ambiguus, homonymus, vagus) does not always have One meaning; as soon as it gets one, its meaning is fixed (terminus fixus). The ambiguity of the expression hinders its certainty §.456, one must therefore prevent all ambiguity. And if the usage of speaking does not suffice for this §.446, one must fix the meanings through logical definitions.
blocks.meier-para-458: The learned expression must please so much that one can thereby be attracted to cognize from it the cognition lying hidden beneath it §.444.30. Consequently it must be adorned with all perfections that are not contrary to learned cognition, so that one reads or hears it gladly and with pleasure.
blocks.meier-para-459: In the use of words in logical definitions four further rules are to be observed: 1) One must also observe the usage of speaking in definitions, as long as it is possible §.455. 2) One must put into the discourse that designates the definition neither the expression of the defined concept, nor its equivalent expressions; for then the definition would be no more distinct than the defined concept §.275, 446. 3) A definition must be expressed with as few words as can be done without detriment to distinctness; so that attention not be distracted by too many words.
blocks.meier-para-460: That meaning for the sake of which a word was invented and is used, even if it should otherwise have no meaning at all, is called the proper meaning (significatus proprius), the other meanings are improper (significatus improprius). If one uses a word to designate the former, it is a proper word (terminus proprius); but if one uses it to designate the latter, it is an improper word (terminus improprius). In an improper word we always think, besides the improper meaning, the proper one, although one could have a detailed concept of each without thinking of the other. Hence one must 4) avoid in the expression of logical definitions all improper expressions, because otherwise the definition would be too extensive §.270, and if we sometimes cannot find proper expressions in the language, we must first transform an improper word into a proper one, through the definition of its improper meaning, before we use it in another definition.
blocks.meier-para-461: If one is to explain the meaning of a word of many meanings, we may explain one among its several meanings that pleases us, if the several meanings are usual to an equal degree. And in this respect definitions are often arbitrary.
blocks.meier-para-462: A judgment that is designated through expressions is called a proposition (propositio, enunciatio). A proposition in which not all concepts are designated with particular expressions is called a hidden proposition (propositio cryptica). The expressions that designate the quantity of the judgment are called the signs of quantity. In a proposition the signs of quantity are either present or not (propositio definita, et indefinita). The latter are understood as universal by linguistic usage, and whoever, therefore, does not want to be misunderstood must not omit the signs of quantity in the propositions that he does not want understood as universal. A proposition is understood when all the expressions found in it are understood §.449.
blocks.meier-para-463: An inference of reason, when it is designated through expressions, is called a syllogistic discourse (syllogismus). One should beware of presenting the syllogistic discourses always in one order, and with the same technical terms. And if one hides or truncates the syllogistic discourses, one should be guided by the hearer, so that he is not led astray and can recall all the omitted propositions. Those fallacies that rest merely on the ambiguity of expressions (sophisma ambiguitatis, amphiboliae) are hardly worth the trouble of mentioning. On the learned style of writing.
blocks.meier-para-464: The learned style of writing (stilus eruditus, philosophicus), is the agreement, or similarity, of the manner and way in which one speaks in a learned fashion.
blocks.meier-para-465: Since the learned style of writing is a part of the learned discourse §.464. 443, it has the same aim as the latter, namely to promote learned cognition in oneself and in others. A good learned style of writing (stilus eruditus perfectus) must therefore promote learned cognition and its perfections, while that which hinders them is a bad learned style of writing (stilus eruditus imperfectus).
blocks.meier-para-466: To the perfections of the learned style of writing belong 1) all its constitutions without which the perfections of learned cognition cannot be maintained; 2) all remaining beauties of the style of writing, if they are not contrary to the perfection of learned cognition. Without these the style of writing would be merely learned. To the imperfections of the learned style of writing belong: 1) all its constitutions by which the perfection of learned cognition is hindered, even should they be beauties; 2) all constitutions by which imperfections in learned cognition are caused; 3) all imperfections that cannot be tolerated in any style of writing §.465.
blocks.meier-para-467: The learned style of writing must be arranged in such a way that through it the distinctness of the cognition of truth from grounds is promoted in the best manner §.465. This is the fundamental law of the learned style of writing.
blocks.meier-para-468: 1) The learned style of writing must be distinct §.467. The distinctness of the learned style of writing (perspicuitas stili eruditi) is its perfection by virtue of which it does not hinder, but promotes the distinctness of the cognition designated. The opposite imperfection is its obscurity (obscuritas stili eruditi). To make the style of writing distinct, one must 1) use nothing but clear expressions §.453-455; 2) one must not speak too briefly, but copiously; 3) one must connect the parts of the discourse with one another so that the connection of the thoughts can be cognized from it most distinctly and easily. Consequently one must a) avoid all rare and difficult constructions; b) not reject the constructions; c) not omit too frequently the expressions that designate the connections of thoughts; d) not make too many insertions; e) not make the periods far too long. A proposition that is not a part of another proposition is called a period (punctum). One must therefore mix shorter and longer periods with one another.
blocks.meier-para-469: 2) The learned style of writing must, as far as is possible, be pure §.467. The purity of the learned style of writing (puritas stili eruditi) consists in its agreement with the improved nature of the language. The opposite imperfection is its impurity (impuritas stili eruditi). Since a pure style of writing pleases, it attracts the attention of the reader and hearer, and it therefore promotes the distinctness of learned cognition §.142.
blocks.meier-para-470: If the purity of the style of writing should hinder its distinctness, one must make an exception from the former §.35. 21. Such a necessary impurity is only an apparent imperfection of the learned style of writing §.466.
blocks.meier-para-471: For the sake of the purity of the learned style of writing one must avoid: 1) all hybrid words (vox hybrida), whose parts are taken from different languages; 2) all grammatical faults; 3) all barbarous expressions; 4) all expressions from foreign languages, and foreign constructions, unless they have already received the right of citizenship; 5) all obsolete expressions and constructions; 6) all new words and technical terms; 7) all multiplicity of expressions, if one can make use of One expression instead of them, although it is impure §.469. From all these rules one can make exceptions for the sake of §.470.
blocks.meier-para-472: With regard to the purity of the learned style of writing there must be avoided: 1) the negligent and heedless barbarism of pedantic scholars, by virtue of which they neglect the purity of the style of writing altogether; 2) the far too great love of purity of the style of writing, when one seeks to maintain the purity quite forcedly, even to the detriment of the perfection of learned cognition §.466.
blocks.meier-para-473: 3) The learned style of writing must, as far as is possible, be fitting. The fittingness of the style of writing (concinnitas stili) consists in the proportioned agreement of the parts of a discourse, e.g. when one forms periods. In a merely learned discourse this perfection cannot be obtained, but in a learned discourse that is not merely learned, one must, in those places where one at the same time thinks beautifully, also take care for this perfection as far as possible §.467. 445, because it makes the expression more agreeable §.458.
blocks.meier-para-474: 4) The learned style of writing must be elegant, as far as is possible §.467. The elegance of the style of writing (ornatus stili eruditi) consists in this, when in place of certain expressions others are used by which just the same concepts, but in a more beautiful way, are designated. In those parts where the discourse is merely learned, no elegant style of writing is possible; but if the learned discourse must at the same time be beautiful, the learned style of writing must also be elegant §.445.
blocks.meier-para-475: 5) The learned style of writing must, as far as is possible, be euphonious §.467. The euphony of the style of writing (sonoritas stili) consists in that perfection by virtue of which it pleases the ears §.458. One must seek this perfection especially in those places of a learned discourse where the discourse is not merely learned §.445.
blocks.meier-para-476: Nothing but simple propositions, and far too extensive periods, obscure the style of writing §.468. In a learned discourse, therefore, also for the sake of the fittingness and euphony of the style of writing §.473. 475, the simple and composite periods must alternate with moderately beautiful periods, according as the thoughts designated are merely learned, or at the same time more or less beautiful.
blocks.meier-para-477: 6) The learned style of writing must, as far as is possible, be suitable §.467. The suitability of the style of writing (congruentia stili) is that perfection by virtue of which the style of writing suits the cognition designated, the speaking person and the hearers, and conforms to them. Consequently the learned style of writing must be important enough for learned cognition §.447, and thus not ridiculous, vulgar, base. And it must be natural to him who makes use of it, and thus not forced.
blocks.meier-para-478: For the sake of the suitability of the learned style of writing it must 1) in those places where one expresses merely learned thoughts, not be so pure, fitting, elegant and euphonious; as 2) in those places where thoughts are expressed that are at the same time beautiful §.477. On a learned discourse.
blocks.meier-para-479: The learned presentation is either an oral presentation, or a written one, that is, a book or a writing (liber, scriptum). Whoever gives a learned presentation is a teacher, and whoever attains his learned cognition from the presentation of another learns it, and is a pupil, whether he be a reader or a hearer.
blocks.meier-para-480: The sense of a learned discourse must be a learned cognition that conforms to all the rules of its perfection §.10-438, and the expression must be so constituted as we have shown thus far §.439-478. We must therefore present in a learned discourse all the parts of learned cognition, and in the sequence in which they must follow upon one another if a learned cognition is to arise.
blocks.meier-para-481: A learned discourse must be extensive in a detailed way §.480. 41-65. It must therefore be neither too brief (oratio erudita nimis brevis), if it says less about the object than suffices for the most perfect learned cognition; nor far too extensive (oratio erudita nimis prolixa), if it says more than is necessary for the attainment of a perfect learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-482: A learned discourse can be too extensive with regard to one, too brief with regard to another, and detailed with regard to a third §.481. Consequently the less capacity a pupil possesses, the less he has already learned, and the less he applies himself to an object, the briefer the learned presentation must be for him. A pupil of the opposite kind must be instructed through a more extensive presentation.
blocks.meier-para-483: A learned discourse must be important enough §.480. 66-91. 447.477. Its object must therefore be no worthless trifle.
blocks.meier-para-484: A learned discourse must be as correct as possible §.480.92-114. 448-452. A scholar who himself errs, and moreover spreads his errors, is a seducer of other people, and doubly imperfect. One must therefore examine one's own cognition most carefully beforehand, before one presents it.
blocks.meier-para-485: A learned discourse must be distinct and intelligible §.480. 114-154. 468. It is therefore a fault 1) if the teacher speaks without understanding, or if his discourse has no sense at all; 2) if his words and constructions are obscure and too difficult; 3) if he himself cannot be understood. A speaker is understood (proponens intelligitur) if one connects with his words just the series of representations that he wanted to designate by them. One can therefore often understand the discourse without understanding the speaker §.449. A teacher must therefore either explain himself in what meanings he takes his words, or he must connect with them no other concepts than those of which he knows that the pupil already has them, and connects them with the words.
blocks.meier-para-486: If a teacher presents confused cognition, his pupil must either already possess it, and he brings it to him through the presentation only into memory, or he must impart it to him in another way than through the presentation. Distinct cognition can be produced in others only through the presentation §.14. A teacher must therefore possess a very distinct cognition.
blocks.meier-para-487: The learned presentation becomes distinct: 1) through a distinct style of writing §.468. 2) Through the observation of a convenient method §.416. 3) When one illustrates abstract cognition through beautiful examples. 4) One should present a matter, if it deserves it on account of its importance, in a manifold and varied way, and make use of aesthetic illustrative arguments. 5) The agreeable and lively in the presentation promotes attention, and thus also distinctness.
blocks.meier-para-488: A learned discourse must be convincing and thorough §.480. 155-215. It is therefore a fault 1) if a teacher offers no proofs at all, when he presents a provable cognition; 2) if his proofs are not certain in the degree, and of the kind of certainty, that the cognition to be presented requires; 3) if he throws blue smoke at his pupils (fucus logicus), that is, if instead of conviction he produces in them a mere persuasion §.184.
blocks.meier-para-489: A learned discourse must be practical §.480. 216-248. Everything that we have so far remarked about the learned discourse must also be applied to the learned presentation §.443.
blocks.meier-para-490: The gift of learned presentation (donum didacticum) is the sum of all skills of the soul and of the body without which no perfect learned presentation is possible. Without this gift no one can be a teacher §.479.
blocks.meier-para-491: A teacher must, in his learned presentation, be guided by his pupils §.479. Consequently one must recommend to him 1) condescension (condescendentia), when he has pupils of lesser capacity before him, and arranges his presentation in such a way that it is not too high for them; 2) elevation (coadscendentia) to the greater capacity of his pupils, so that the presentation not be too poor for them.
blocks.meier-para-492: A pupil of learned cognition 1) must by nature be disposed to learned cognition; 2) he must already have exercised his understanding; 3) he must often already possess a store of learned cognition; 4) he must apply the necessary diligence to the learning of learned cognition. A scholar must therefore present learned cognition to no one except one who is a skilful pupil of it; and he must not become angry when he sees that some people learn nothing from his presentation, unless he turn his anger against himself, because he sees that he is applying his effort to the wrong persons.
blocks.meier-para-493: In a learned presentation one has either chiefly the aim of refuting someone and his error, and it is then a refutation of another (refutatio alterius), or not. In the latter case one regards the reader or hearer as a pupil who is ignorant, but not as one in error, and one therefore seeks to produce a perfect learned cognition in him; such a presentation is called instruction (docere).
blocks.meier-para-494: In learned instruction the following rules must be observed: 1) One must make the beginning with the definition or description of all concepts that occur in the object, if they are not otherwise already sufficiently clear to the pupil; and one must convince him of the correctness of these concepts according to the rules of the 258. 265. 267. and 278th paragraph.
blocks.meier-para-495: 2) In instruction about an unprovable proposition one needs nothing further than to analyze it, and, if it can be done, to illustrate it through an example §.313-318. 300. 487.
blocks.meier-para-496: 3) In instruction about an intuitive judgment one must either call back into the pupil's memory all the sensations of which this judgment consists; or one must impart them to him in the instruction §.319-321. 202; or one must convince him through probable testimonies that others have had these sensations §.206-215.
blocks.meier-para-497: 4) In instruction concerning provable propositions, a) one should analyse the proposition and the solution of a problem, so that they may be properly understood; b) one should present the proof according to the analytic method, and, if it is long, bring it into one or a couple of formal syllogisms §.423. 203. 204. 206-215; c) one should carry the whole proof on until one arrives either at unprovable and intuitive judgments, or at such provable judgments of which the other is already sufficiently convinced. Hence the citation of the paragraphs in writings.
blocks.meier-para-498: 5) One should seal the conviction of the truth by a practical representation of its practical character: for what the heart loves, the understanding believes §.216-248.
blocks.meier-para-499: A correct proof that an error is an error is a true refutation (refutatio vera); but an incorrect proof that an error is an error, or that a truth is an error, is an apparent refutation (impugnatio). Only errors can be correctly refuted. He who undertakes the refutation is the attacking party (adversarius opponens), and he who refutes the refutation is the defending party (adversarius defendens). The defence is therefore either correct or false. A learned dispute (controversia) consists in the refutation and defence of an opinion.
blocks.meier-para-500: The proposition that the attacking party refutes and the attacked party defends is called the disputed proposition (thesis controversa), and the proposition of the attacking party that cannot be true at the same time as the disputed proposition is called the counter-proposition (antithesis). It is therefore opposed to the disputed proposition either in a contradictory manner §.343, or in a general manner §.345. The point at issue is determined (status controversiae, seu quaestionis formatur) when the attacking party clearly demonstrates which is the disputed proposition and which is the counter-proposition.
blocks.meier-para-501: If the point at issue is not correctly determined, then the opponents either conduct no dispute at all, or they fall into a dispute about words (logomachia), that is, into a dispute that arises because one does not understand the other §.500, and that is always a foolish and futile business. Different from these, however, are disputes about words (controversia philologica), which are true disputes, whose object, however, is words or other expressions.
blocks.meier-para-502: Learned disputes must be conducted according to the following rules: 1) The attacking party should seek a fault in the proof of his opponent §.194, or in general a deviation of the opponent's thoughts from the rules of logic. He has then indeed not refuted the matter itself, but yet his opponent's way of thinking. Against such an attack one cannot defend oneself at all, if it is correct; or one must show that one has not violated the rules of logic, the transgression of which has been imputed to us.
blocks.meier-para-503: 2) If the attacking party demonstrates the counter-proposition, it follows from this that the disputed proposition is false and that the opponent errs §.500. Against this attack one can defend oneself only if the opponent has committed a fault in his demonstration, and this one must show according to the first rule §.502. If one party can show the other that it accepts provable propositions without proof, this objection remains unanswered until this proof is furnished.
blocks.meier-para-504: 3) The attacking party refutes the disputed proposition by an apagogic proof §.196. To this belongs also the case when one shows that the disputed proposition contradicts another opinion of the opponent, although we do not accept that opinion ourselves (argumentatio ad hominem). Against such an attack one can defend oneself only if there is a fault in the apagogic proof, and this one must show to the opponent §.502.
blocks.meier-para-505: 4) If one of the opponents abandons the point at issue and brings forward things by which the disputed proposition is not refuted and the counter-proposition is not proved, then one must not engage with such matters but concede them in the present dispute, so that it does not become far too prolix §.481. The other party can in this case defend itself only if the first has conceded something through haste, and then it must show that what was conceded does indeed concern the point at issue.
blocks.meier-para-506: 5) The attacking party can show, by a limitation §.299 that he adds to the disputed proposition, that it is not as universally true as the opponent gives it out to be. Against this attack we can defend ourselves only by showing either that this limitation has no influence on the present point at issue, or that it is false, or by soundly proving that our proposition is true without limitation.
blocks.meier-para-507: 6) The attacking party brings a distinction (distinctio) to bear against his opponent, or he shows the difference between the things that the opponent has confounded, and through the confounding of which he has been misled into entering a dispute, or into erring. Against a distinction one can defend oneself just as against a limitation §.506.
blocks.meier-para-508: 7) The attacking party can refute the universality of the disputed propositions by instances. An instance (instantia) is an exception to a proposition, from which it sufficiently appears that it is not universally true. Against an instance one can defend oneself only if one either accepts it, or shows that it does not fit, or so limits the disputed proposition that it does not fit; or demonstrates the universality of the disputed proposition without regard to the instance.
blocks.meier-para-509: 8) The attacked party uses reprisals (retorsio) when he shows that what the opponent has derived from the disputed proposition by the apagogic proof §.504 follows rather from the counter-proposition. And then the attacking party can defend himself in no other way than by showing that his opponent commits a fault in his proof.
blocks.meier-para-510: 9) After the refutation is completed, one should seek to instil in the opponent an abhorrence of the error, by showing, yet without violating the duties one owes to the opponent, that it is dangerous, harmful and ridiculous. Against this attack one can defend oneself only by showing that the opponent regards our opinion from the wrong side. Through a correct observance of these rules, refutations become at the same time practical §.489.
blocks.meier-para-511: If one derives bad and absurd consequences from the disputed proposition, not in order to convince the opponent of his error, but to offend him in some way, then one is a consequence-maker (consequentiarius). Consequence-making is not necessarily a fault against logic, but it is always a sin, and therefore deserves to be abhorred by all honest people.
blocks.meier-para-512: The defence against a consequence-maker is called the justification (apologia); one can conduct it either with logical weapons, if the consequence-maker has committed faults against logic §.511, in which case one must at the same time show him his folly and wicked heart, yet without consequence-making; or one must avail oneself of the weapons of law, and then logic has nothing more to remark on the matter.
blocks.meier-para-513: Although learned disputes have utility §.178, a scholar must nevertheless 1) make no trade of refuting others; 2) begin no dispute of his own over a trifle; 3) conduct the important and necessary refutations with perfect thoroughness, and 4) not defend himself against all attacks.
blocks.meier-para-514: Two disputing parties dispute with one another (disputatio formaliter sumta) when the counter-proposition is presented and assessed in a learned manner, and when both take place orally and in the presence of both parties. He who presents the counter-proposition in a learned manner is the opponent (opponens), and he who assesses it, that is, discovers what is false and uncertain in it and in its proof, is the respondent (respondens). So that disputing may not become disorderly and far too prolix, only the opponent must furnish proofs, and the respondent must do nothing further than assess the proofs.
blocks.meier-para-515: Since the speeches that are delivered in disputing do not belong to the domain of logic, it is clear that the opponent makes the beginning of the disputation, and then he must 1) determine the point at issue §.500. 501. If he does not understand the opinion of the respondent, he must have it explained to him by the latter. 2) He should attack the respondent according to one of the rules set out in §.502-510. 3) For the sake of brevity and clarity, he should present his proofs in formal syllogisms §.399, and 4) for the same reason he should make use of the analytic method §.423. The Socratic and Platonic method makes disputing too prolix and burdensome §.430. Unless one were to see oneself compelled, by the first, to keep the other party to the point at issue.
blocks.meier-para-516: The respondent accepts the argument (assumere argumentum) when he repeats the objection of the opponent, and this is useful in order to consider it properly, so that he can answer it soundly.
