For the sake of brevity the respondent must do nothing further than show where the opponent has committed a fault either in the matter or in the form of his proof §.502, and then he must demand that the opponent either change his inference of reason, or prove the premise that seems to the respondent false or uncertain.
blocks.meier-para-517: The assistant of the respondent (praeses) is to prevent the respondent from conceding the counter-proposition that has not yet been sufficiently proved. He must therefore, when the respondent knows nothing more, or nothing skilful, to answer, take over his office §.516. On learned writings.
blocks.meier-para-518: The presentation of past events is history (historia). Learned writings present either history or dogmatic truths §.104. The former are historical (scripta erudita historica), and the latter dogmatic writings (scripta dogmatica). These present either a common cognition of dogmatic truths, or a learned one §.18. 21. The former are historical-dogmatic (scriptum historico-dogmaticum), the latter, however, systematic writings (scriptum systematicum), which are scientific writings (scriptum scientificum) if they present a science §.434. Every writing is, in regard to its content, either very extensive or very brief. The former is a great work (systema), the latter, however, an epitome (compendium).
blocks.meier-para-519: History narrates either things that belong to nature and art, insofar as one considers in them neither the free actions of human beings nor their closer effects; or it narrates the free actions of human beings, together with everything that stands in a closer connection with them. The former is the history of nature and art (historia naturae et artis), the latter, however, history simply (historia stricte dicta). To the last belongs 1) political history (historia politica), which narrates the civil and political actions of human beings; 2) ecclesiastical history (historia ecclesiastica), which narrates the fortunes of the churches and the actions of human beings that have a noticeable influence on them; 3) private history (historia privata), which narrates the course of life of individual persons, insofar as it has no noticeable influence on the state, the church and learning; 4) learned history (historia litteraria), which narrates the events of the learned world, and it is either a history of the disciplines, or of the learned, or of learned writings.
blocks.meier-para-520: A historical writing must be 1) detailed §.481.482, neither too prolix nor too brief. It can therefore be detailed for one purpose and for one reader, too prolix for another purpose and for another reader, and too brief for a third purpose and for a third reader. With time every history becomes too brief. 2) Important, both as regards the whole content and as regards that which is narrated of it §.483. 3) Correct §.484. 4) Distinct §.485, hence paintings and copperplate engravings are often necessary. 5) Thorough §.488, consequently proving everything according to the rules of paragraphs 206-215. 6) Practical or pragmatic (historia pragmatica) §.489. 7) Methodical §.487. 432.
blocks.meier-para-521: If history is to be pragmatic and detailed at the same time, it must be presented in such a way that a purpose is attained that is practical enough §.520. Now since everything that is actual in this world, if it can be cognised by us human beings, aims not only at the honour of GOD but also at our happiness, a writer of history must seek to attain these two purposes through history. In particular, in natural history one must have a twofold purpose §.519: 1) to come to know better the perfections of GOD from natural things, and 2) to impart to readers distinct concepts of natural things, and thereby to pave the way to learned cognition of them.
blocks.meier-para-522: History in the narrower sense §.519 redounds to the honour of GOD if one recognises, from the events of human beings, the divine government of the human race, and the perfections that GOD reveals in it. To the happiness of human beings contributes 1) civil history, if one can learn from it political prudence in the affairs of war and peace; 2) ecclesiastical history, if one can learn from it the prudence of governing the church, and if it develops the marks of the true and the false church; 3) learned history, if it promotes learning; 4) private history, if one can learn from it human prudence in private life.
blocks.meier-para-523: The historical-dogmatic writings are not learned writings §.518. But if they are detailed, important, comprehensible, correct and practical, they are very useful to people who cannot and will not be made learned, likewise also to children who are to be introduced to the sciences, in order to instil in them a foretaste of learning.
blocks.meier-para-524: A systematic book must be 1) detailed §.481. 482. It must therefore either contain everything that was known of a doctrine at the time the book was written, or it must contain as much of it as the particular purpose of the author requires. The most detailed writings can in time become undetailed, and one must therefore carefully distinguish from one another the detailedness of a dogmatic book in respect of time, author and reader; 2) important §.483; 3) correct §.484, in that not only are all the thoughts contained in it true, but each is also in conformity with the rules of logic. 4) Distinct and comprehensible §.485. 5) Thorough §.488, it must therefore be written according to the learned method and coherently. 6) Practical §.489. 7) Methodical §.414-438.
blocks.meier-para-525: Botching together (compilatio) consists in this, that an author writes together everything he finds here and there on the matter he wants to write about, without properly connecting it with one another. Although a botched-together work can be useful to other scholars, it nevertheless remains, in regard to the author, a wretched work. A writing is stolen together (plagiarius) when the author gives himself out as the inventor of those thoughts that he has learned from others.
blocks.meier-para-526: He who makes an epitome of a great work (epitomator), by omitting from it everything that is superfluous with regard to his smaller aim, can write a very useful and necessary book, provided he has chosen his purpose reasonably §.518. On the character of a scholar.
blocks.meier-para-527: The character of a scholar (character eruditi) consists in the sum total of those of his marks that are the nearer grounds and causes of learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-528: The general character of a scholar (generalis character eruditi) is the character of a scholar insofar as it contains the nearer grounds of learning in general; the special, however (character eruditi specialis), insofar as it contains the nearer grounds of this or that kind, and of this or that part of learning.
blocks.meier-para-529: The first part of the general character of a scholar consists in the learned natural disposition (natura erudita), or in that proportion of all powers of the soul by virtue of which a human being is fitted and inclined for learned cognition §.528.
blocks.meier-para-530: To the learned natural disposition belongs 1) native wit, the learned head (ingenium eruditum), the proportion of the powers of cognition by which a human being is fitted for learned cognition. To this belongs a) reason (ratio), the faculty of distinctly seeing the connection of things §.21, which must be naturally disposed to become sound, widely extended, strong, thorough and beautiful. b) The understanding (intellectus), the faculty of distinct cognition §.21. 17, which must be naturally disposed to become widely extended, profound, pure and beautiful. Consequently great attention, reflection, consideration and abstraction belong to native wit §.142. 2) A beautiful mind (ingenium pulchrum), the proportion of the powers of cognition by virtue of which a human being is disposed to beautiful thinking §.32.
blocks.meier-para-531: To the learned natural disposition belongs 2) the learned temperament (temperamentum eruditum), or the proportion of the faculties of desire, and their agreement with native wit, by virtue of which a human being is not only inclined to attain a learned cognition, but by virtue of which also the powers of cognition are duly exerted to effect the most perfect learned cognition §.529.
blocks.meier-para-532: The learned natural disposition is a mere gift of fortune, which must be innate in a human being, and without which it is impossible to attain learned cognition anywhere by any art.
blocks.meier-para-533: Native wit is called the innate natural logic (logica naturalis connata), but the science of learned cognition and of learned presentation, scholastic wit, or artificial logic (logica artificialis). The indistinct cognition of the rules of native wit, together with the skill of observing them, which one acquires by the mere use of native wit, is called acquired natural logic (logica naturalis acquisita theoretica et practica), and one reckons it to native wit in the wider sense. Native wit does not contradict scholastic wit; it is indispensable to the latter both in theory and in practice. It is also sufficient outside the disciplines. But without scholastic wit no learned cognition can be attained; it improves native wit, and if a great scholastic wit is joined with a great native wit, a human being can get much further than by the best native wit taken alone.
blocks.meier-para-534: He who wants to become a great scholar must follow nature, and apply himself to learned cognition only if he possesses the learned natural disposition, and insofar as he possesses it §.532.
blocks.meier-para-535: One can recognise whether one possesses the learned natural disposition: 1) if one has a reasonable inclination to learned cognition, because its perfections delight us; 2) if it goes easily for us whenever we think in a learned way; 3) if one becomes aware by an attempt that one can actually think in a learned way.
blocks.meier-para-536: The second part of the general character of a scholar consists in the skills that he gradually attains through exercises §.527. To the skills of a scholar belong: 1) The extension of the understanding and of reason (extensio intellectus et rationis), the skill of cognising many things distinctly and in a manifold connection, and of cognising many clear marks of each thing §.25. 2) The strength of reason and of the understanding (intensio intellectus et rationis), the skill of cognising things in a great degree of completeness and mathematical certainty §.27. 28.29. 3) The skill of thinking beautifully §.32 4) A great heart §.91 (magnitudo pectoris), the skill of thinking and acting in accordance with the learned temperament §.531, which presupposes the skill of thinking in no other way than greatly and practically §.26. 30.
blocks.meier-para-537: The learned exercises are A) the more general (exercitia generaliora), the frequent repetitions of learned meditation in general. To this belongs 1) learned naturalising, the exercises one undertakes without art, and which make up acquired natural logic §.433.
blocks.meier-para-538: 2) The more perfect, regular and artificial exercises (exercitia oculatiora, logica artificialis practica), or the frequent observance of the rules of artificial logic. To this end a) one should learn a good artificial logic; b) one should seek to practise all its rules; c) when one has produced and written down a series of thoughts according to the logical rules, one should hold them against these rules, and examine where one has observed them or not. Through these exercises one must finally bring it about that one observes the rules of artificial logic in thinking and speaking without being conscious of them.
blocks.meier-para-539: B) The special learned exercises, or studying (exercitia erudita specialiora), consists in all actions by which learned cognition arises and is improved in him who undertakes these actions. Six exercises belong to this.
blocks.meier-para-540: I) Learning from an oral presentation. Because this exercise is the easiest and surest, one must make the beginning with it. He who wants to be taught by this exercise must 1) have prepared his head for learning through the lower and beautiful sciences. 2) He must seek out a teacher at least moderately competent, from whose oral presentation he can hope to attain a good learned cognition. 3) He must pay proper attention to the oral presentation, so that he may rightly understand the teacher and his presentation. 4) He must meditate through everything the teacher presents, or at least the main points of his presentation §.436. 437. 5) He must judge logically (logice diiudicare) everything he has heard, that is, seek to recognise what logical perfections or imperfections are found in it. Hence he must investigate to what kind and species of learned cognition that belongs which he wants to judge; he must recall the logical rules of this kind or species, and seek to recognise, from the comparison of the object with these rules, whether it is in conformity with them or not.
blocks.meier-para-541: II) The reading of learned writings. To this end one must a) set before oneself a reasonable purpose for the sake of which one wants to read learned writings. A student must therefore read books 1) in order to review a discipline that one has already learned; 2) in order to improve our learned cognition more and more; 3) in order to learn a part of learning that one does not yet understand; 4) in order to practise oneself in the observance of the rules of logic. b) One must choose a book that is suited to promote this purpose. Consequently one must 1) not read all books as they happen to fall into one's hands. 2) In the beginning read only such books as one has found, after a logical judgment, to be suited to promote our purpose. 3) If one already possesses a skill in thinking in a learned way, one can also read with profit such books as are full of defects and faults. c) One must seek to understand the book and the author rightly. d) One must meditate through and logically judge every thought presented in the book, as in §.540. n. 4. 5, so that one may learn rightly to see into the things presented.
blocks.meier-para-542: The useful reading of learned writings is promoted by the observance of the following rules: 1) One should read with the greatest attention, without tolerating foreign thoughts. 2) One should read the book through from the beginning, if it is written systematically. 3) One should never interrupt the reading in a closely connected matter. 4) One should read the book through hastening slowly, and neither too quickly nor too slowly. 5) One must not become weary of reading before one has come to the end. 6) One must not read too many books, especially of differing content, intermingled with one another. 7) One should make the beginning with the shorter epitomes, proceed to the greater works, and finally read writings that treat particular matters in detail. 8) One should read the writings that belong to a principal part of learning according to the synthetic method.
blocks.meier-para-543: The learning of learned cognition is greatly promoted, partly if at first one learns the elements of the learning to which one has devoted oneself from only One teacher; partly if one at once employs the truths learned and brings them to practice.
blocks.meier-para-544: III) Frequent repetition (repetitio), or recollection of what one has learned. For this it is required that one observe the following rules: 1) One must not make of this repetition a mere learning by heart. 2) In the repetition one must meditate through and judge every thought just as if one wanted to learn it for the first time, even though this always goes more briskly and easily. 3) One should repeat the truths learned according to the synthetic method according to the analytic and inferential method §.423. 428. 4) One should repeat the repetition often, with some variation. 5) One should always learn more besides, and practise the truths learned. 6) If one writes down one's meditations in the repetition, this exercise is thereby greatly promoted. 7) One should present the truths learned, in writing or orally, in a learned manner. 8) One should converse with others about the truths learned.
blocks.meier-para-545: The repetition and the learning of learned cognition is greatly promoted if one writes down briefly, and with a reasonable choice, that which one fears to forget, and which at the same time brings the rest back to our memory.
blocks.meier-para-546: IV) Investigation (investigatio), or the reasonable imitation of other scholars in their learned thinking and presentation. To this end 1) one should choose a great scholar as a model to follow. 2) One should investigate how he manages to think so learnedly, so thoroughly, so orderly, etc. 3) One should investigate how he discovered the truths, or how they could be discovered if they had not yet been found. 4) One should seek to think and to speak in the same way in similar cases.
blocks.meier-para-547: V) One should present the disciplines to others in a learned manner, either orally or in writing. Or learned presentation is an exercise in learned cognition; for by teaching we learn.
blocks.meier-para-548: VI) The invention of new truths (inventio), when we cognise something in a learned way without learning it from other human beings; whether we be the first human beings to cognise it, or others may already have known it before us. This exercise is the most difficult, and must be put off until last.
blocks.meier-para-549: An autodidact is a scholar who has been taught without a teacher, whether he has either invented all his learning §.548, or has merely received no oral instruction. A reasonable human being chooses the easiest and surest way when he first seeks to learn from an oral presentation, then reads books, and rather applies his power of invention to discovering wholly new truths than such as have long been known, if all this is otherwise only possible for him.
blocks.meier-para-550: Just as it is a fault to want to be made learned without native wit §.534; so it is a negligent way of thinking in a learned manner (negligens eruditionis genus et impolitum) if one does not duly combine art with native wit §.533.
blocks.meier-para-551: The affected and forced way of thinking in a learned manner (affectatum et coactum eruditionis genus) arises when scholastic wit is combined with native wit in a bad manner: 1) if the rules of artificial logic are false and ungrounded; 2) if its correct rules are badly applied, in that they are not suited either to the truths or to the natural disposition of the scholar.
blocks.meier-para-552: A cognition and a presentation that are merely learned are the dry, sober, rough, scholastic and pedantic kind of learning (macilentum, ieiunum, pedanticum, scholasticum eruditionis genus). In order to prevent this, a student must daily devote some time, in the hours of recreation, to the beautiful sciences.
blocks.meier-para-553: The third part of the general character of a scholar consists in learned diligence (diligentia erudita), or in as great an exertion of all acquired learned skills as is required in each case when one wants to think and present in a learned way in a certain degree of perfection §.527. To this end one must observe ten rules.
blocks.meier-para-554: 1) A student must, above all things, mark out the horizon of his learned cognition as accurately as possible, so that he may know in each case on what he has to direct his learned diligence. And so that this horizon may be assumed neither too small nor too large, one must gradually extend it further, as our powers and skills increase.
blocks.meier-para-555: 2) A student must judge his powers most exactly, as to whether they suffice for learning in general, and for that part of it to which he applies himself, and for the cognition of this or that truth. To this end a) he must test himself as to whether he possesses the learned natural disposition §.529-535. b) One should transform that with regard to which one wants to test one's powers into a problem §.328-339, and examine whether one has powers enough to actually effect the solution. c) One should guard against the prejudice of too great confidence and of mistrust in the judgment of one's powers §.170. d) One should test one's powers by a faithful trial. e) One should let oneself be judged by others.
blocks.meier-para-556: 3) In studying one must not apply too much diligence, and must not direct learned diligence to things that are found above, below and outside the horizon of our learned cognition §.554.
blocks.meier-para-557: 4) One must also not apply too little diligence, but as much as is required to undertake all learned exercises duly, and gradually to study through the whole horizon of our learned cognition.
blocks.meier-para-558: 5) One must begin to study as early as is possible; what one wants to do, one should do soon.
blocks.meier-para-559: 6) One must, if it is otherwise possible for us, study daily, and think in a learned way. He who does not go further forward goes backward.
blocks.meier-para-560: 7) One must, in the midst of the course of studying, always hasten slowly. So that one may not hasten too much, one must not leave a learned occupation until one has satisfied all the rules of logic in it. But so that one may also not be too slow, one must duly spur on the desire to study.
blocks.meier-para-561: 8) One must never cease to learn, in that one either always learns something new besides, or learns to cognise better what has already been learned.
blocks.meier-para-562: 9) One must constantly seek to improve the learning one has already attained, and to remove its still outstanding defects and faults.
blocks.meier-para-563: 10) One must combine with studying daily experience, intercourse with the respectable world, and the use of the very things on which one meditates in a learned way; so that one may not, as a mere learned worm, live on school-dust, and dream of Platonic republics.
